#5645. The US Is Auctioning Seabed Near American Samoa. A $3 Million Bid Will Not Build a Mine.

On November 19, the US Marine Minerals Administration is scheduled to auction mineral rights covering about 31.5 million acres of seabed near American Samoa. The two areas have minimum bids of $3 million apiece, with 20-year lease terms. It is an impressive area and a modest opening price for a prospective new metals industry. The difference between the two numbers helps explain what the sale is actually offering.

The winning bidder will acquire a position from which to study mineral deposits and seek subsequent permissions. The government has said explicitly that an issued lease does not authorize commercial harvesting. It allows preliminary work such as mapping, while physical exploration, testing and mining require additional plans and approvals. The lease does not establish reserves, a collector that can work for years, a processing plant or buyers willing to pay enough for the metals.

The announcement is being treated as an American critical-minerals milestone. Investors should pay close attention to the difference between a government auction and an operating mining project. A mineral lease can have speculative value long before a profitable business exists.

In my new TFIE Strategy Briefing on the American Samoa auction, I examine how federal leasing can advance while the integrated business case remains weak.

The acreage has no direct relationship to the amount of commercially recoverable metal. The final federal notice describes northern and southern areas of roughly 16.3 million and 15.2 million acres. They are regulatory boundaries. A mining company needs deposit-grade and abundance data, continuity, recoverable tonnage, processing recoveries and a market price that leaves a margin after all the offshore and downstream costs.

The geology is becoming better understood. In April 2026, US Geological Survey scientists deployed 38 box cores in the Samoa Basin, of which 36 yielded enough material for nodule-density measurements. The expedition report is useful new evidence about the region. It is an expedition summary rather than a reserve statement for either lease area. Mineral distributions vary within the sampled region, and the better-studied Clarion-Clipperton Zone is not an adequate substitute for American Samoa’s own geological evidence.

Collection creates another set of costs. Impossible Metals proposes autonomous vehicles that select nodules and return to a support vessel. The Metals Company uses a more mature crawler-and-riser approach that has demonstrated recovery at pilot scale. Both must turn offshore demonstrations into dependable annual production, with maintenance, ship time, recovery systems and delays included. Their technologies should not be assigned the same engineering maturity, but neither has proved a profitable integrated mining-and-processing business.

In 2025, metallurgical engineer Lyle Trytten and I completed an independent techno-economic assessment commissioned by the National Ocean Protection Coalition. We examined both collection approaches, offshore operations, processing, metal markets and financial sensitivities. We judged commercial viability within the following 15 years highly unlikely. A new leasing process has not supplied the operating and financial evidence that was missing in that assessment.

The history of first-of-a-kind offshore production should influence the financing. Nautilus Minerals spent substantial capital on its Solwara-1 venture without reaching commercial production. Deep-sea mining depends on specialized machines, ships, handling systems, processing capacity and sales contracts working in sequence. The first production years of comparable projects are rarely smooth. The lease is one of the cheapest and earliest commitments in that chain.

American Samoa also has its own decision to make. Its government has supported scientific investigation while withholding support for commercial extraction at present. A lawsuit filed by Samoan chiefs and community groups contests the federal process. The resulting legal and territorial questions matter alongside engineering and economics. The environmental finding for preliminary leasing activities is not a finding about the effects of a future commercial mine.

Auction results will show what qualified bidders will pay for an opportunity. A winning bid can justify a company’s further studies and improve its fundraising story. An operating business will require years of capital investment, production evidence and profitable metal sales. Those are much harder milestones, and they remain ahead of the bidders.

Read A Seabed Lease Does Not Fix a Broken Business Case for the full assessment of the auction, and the Barnard–Trytten report for the underlying engineering and financial analysis.

“Brigham nurses have made clear that we are prepared to stay on strike for as long as it takes to win a contract that protects our patients and respects the nurses who care for them,” Kelly Morgan, a labor and delivery nurse and chair of the Brigham and Women’s Hospital MNA Bargaining Committee, said in the union’s announcement. “An open-ended strike is a serious step that will undoubtedly create a healthcare crisis in Massachusetts. The hospital has previously said it has found agreements with the union on several issues. MGB is the largest private employer in Massachusetts with roughly 85,000 workers and $22.8 billion in annual revenue, making it among the country’s largest nonprofit health systems. #5643. Shorter Cycle Maintains Efficacy of Colorectal Cancer Regimen

— 14-day cycle length for trifluridine-tipiracil plus bevacizumab also limited toxicity

A shorter cycle length for a standard treatment for refractory metastatic colorectal cancer was noninferior to the typical longer length for overall survival (OS), while limiting toxicity, the phase III PRABITAS trial from Japan showed.

Median OS was 10.3 months in patients who received the standard 28-day cycle length of trifluridine-tipiracil (FTD-TPI; Lonsurf) and bevacizumab versus 11.3 months for those who received a 14-day schedule (stratified HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.80-1.08), reported Hiroya Taniguchi, MD, of Aichi Cancer Center Hospital in Nagoya, and colleagues.

This met the prespecified noninferiority margin of below 1.25 for the upper limit of the confidence interval, they noted in The Lancet.

The 12-month OS rates were 44% in the 28-day group and 47.5% in the 14-day group.

Importantly, rates of grade ≥3 neutropenia and grade ≥2 anorexia were reduced in the shorter-course group.

"Taken together with previous evidence, these findings support adoption of the 14-day FTD-TPI plus bevacizumab schedule as the preferred standard of care for refractory metastatic colorectal cancer," Taniguchi and colleagues wrote.

FTD-TPI plus bevacizumab was established as the standard treatment for refractory metastatic colorectal cancer based on results from the phase III SUNLIGHT trial, in which patients treated with the regimen achieved a significant improvement in OS compared with FTD-TPI monotherapy. Data from a real-world analysis supported the SUNLIGHT results.

However, Taniguchi and colleagues noted that while the regimen -- which involves administering FTD-TPI twice daily on days 1-5 and 8-12, and bevacizumab on days 1 and 15 of a 28-day cycle -- was generally tolerable, it "carries a treatment burden that leaves room for further optimization."

In particular, it has been associated with increased hematologic toxicity, including grade ≥3 neutropenia.

"The clinical message stemming from PRABITAS is straightforward," wrote Paolo Ciracì, MD, and Chiara Cremolini, MD, PhD, of Azienda Ospedaliera Universitaria Pisana in Pisa, Italy, in an accompanying commentary. "Simplifying FTD-TPI administration in a 14-day schedule does not compromise treatment efficacy but does reduce the burden of adverse events and also the complexity of treatment delivery."

The study also reflects a move towards a more patient-centered approach by "shifting the focus from which therapies should be used, and in what sequence, to how effective therapies can be delivered to preserve patients' fitness and their ability to remain on treatment and receive subsequent lines," they added.

However, Ciracì and Cremolini noted that it remains an open question whether these results translate into a meaningful improvement in quality of life since Taniguchi and colleagues did not formally assess that endpoint.

Given that a 14-day schedule had been proposed to reduce toxicity, the researchers sought to determine whether the shorter course was noninferior to the conventional 28-day schedule for OS.

PRABITAS was conducted at 178 hospitals in Japan and included 972 patients assigned to receive FTD-TPI (35 mg/m2 orally twice daily) plus bevacizumab (5 mg/kg intravenously) on either a conventional 28-day schedule or a 14-day cycle schedule (FTD-TPI on days 1-5, and bevacizumab on day 1).

Median patient age was 68 years, the majority (57%) were men, and RAS mutations were present in 59% of patients. The median follow-up was 17.9 months.

Looking at secondary endpoints, median progression-free survival was 3.9 months in both groups (stratified HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81-1.06). The median time to treatment failure was 3.6 months in the 28-day group and 3.8 months in the 14-day group (stratified HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.79-1.03).

Among 906 patients with measurable disease at baseline, the objective response rate was 2.4% in the 28-day group and 1.6% in the 14-day group, with no complete responses observed. The disease control rate was 46.6% and 52.1% in the two groups, respectively.

Grade ≥3 neutropenia occurred in 39% of patients in the 28-day group and 13% in the 14-day group, with grade 4 neutropenia occurring in 8% and 1%, respectively. Febrile neutropenia occurred in 5% of patients in the 28-day group versus 1% in the 14-day group.

Non-hematologic toxicities were also less frequent in the 14-day group.

Grade ≥2 anorexia occurred in 26% of patients in the 28-day group compared with 15% in the 14-day group, while nausea was reported in 18% and 12%, respectively, and diarrhea in 10% and 4%.

Two treatment-related deaths occurred in the 14-day group, including one gastrointestinal hemorrhage and one gastrointestinal perforation, both attributed to bevacizumab.

#5642. ONC, CMS move electronic prior authorization into real-world testing

ONC, CMS move electronic prior authorization into real-world testing" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) is launching a voluntary industry testing initiative to help healthcare organizations prepare for federal electronic prior authorization requirements taking effect in 2027.

ONC is collaborating with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) to launch a series of industry testing events in production-like environments to advance end-to-end electronic prior authorization (ePA), the agencies announced Thursday.

A federal rule requires some payers to implement an application programming interface (API) to support electronic prior authorization processes by January 1. Impacted payers include Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, CHIP and ACA exchange plans.

The focused, 10- to 12-week testing sprints will bring together payers, providers, hospitals, electronic health record (EHR) developers, intermediaries and other industry partners to test their own workflows across connected systems and identify gaps before broader implementation, CMS and ONC officials said.

"Federal regulations and industry standards have laid important groundwork for ePA, but our work is not done," Tom Keane, M.D., National Coordinator for Health IT, said in a statement. "With our colleagues at CMS, we are bringing partners together to advance the next phase of implementation testing to accelerate ePA progress in the near term."

Organizations interested in participating can learn more and sign up for the initiative by November 20, according to ONC. Participant feedback and lessons learned will inform future testing and implementation activities.

"Regulations and industry standards have laid important groundwork for ePA, but real work remains to put this policy into practice. These events mark the next phase of implementation testing, bringing trading partners together to examine end-to-end workflows in production-like environments," ONC leaders Ashley Hain and Molly Prieto, principal deputy director of the Office of Standards, Certification and Analysis, wrote in a blog post.

During the testing sprints, participants will use their own workflows to examine how prior authorization requests and decisions move across connected systems. "The focus is on finding technical barriers and workflow gaps that could arise in real-world implementation, while organizations still have an opportunity to address them before broader deployment," Hain and Prieto wrote.

ONC and CMS will use the findings from the testing events to make practical improvements. "Some findings may point to standards that need clarification or revision. Others may reveal a need for clearer educational materials for developers, providers and hospitals, or more useful implementer guidance," Hain and Prieto wrote.

"We aim to identify critical updates quickly and help industry prioritize the improvements needed for successful implementation across care settings. The purpose is to turn the progress already made through regulations and standards into workflows that reduce administrative burden and support timely care," the ONC leaders wrote.

The testing events will include workflows and real-world scenarios using the HL7 FHIR Da Vinci implementation guides for Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD), Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR), and Prior Authorization Support (PAS). Each event will include coordinated scenarios, based on high-volume clinical services that require prior authorization and supporting resources to help participants test together, ONC said.

ONC and CMS are working with the MITRE-led Health Federally Funded Research and Development Center and Drummond Group to support stakeholder recruitment, readiness discussions, participant matching and testing coordination. Drummond Group will operate FHIRplace, the virtual environment where developers, providers, payers and intermediaries will test with their trading partners.

CMS and ONC encouraged participation from organizations of all sizes, including smaller organizations and those serving rural communities.

#5641. Zoox Launches Robotaxis in Atlanta

The year of the robotaxi rolls on. Just after writing about Zoox expanding its robotaxi service in Las Vegas, I see news that Zoox is entering Atlanta!

“Our initial rollout will focus on the Northwest region of Atlanta, near Atlantic Station, Woodward, and Home Park. We will expand throughout the year as our testing progresses,” Zoox shares.

To start with, in order to work out any bugs and avoid controversy, the service can only be used by Zoox employees, family members, and friends. But that should change fairly soon. “We look forward to opening our waitlist for Atlanta in the coming months, ahead of the launch of our Zoox Explorers early rider program.”

I do find it interesting that Zoox, Waymo, and Tesla are all in a sort of fast (but sort of small) expansion phase at the same time. They each keep adding more cities, but with quite limited geographic ranges and vehicle fleets. Is it all the early budding of robotaxi services that will bloom into giant networks? Or is it companies rushing to try to prove their viability and build up economies of scale, but which might not actually be financially viable and profitable in the long run — or even next year? We’ll have to wait to see. In the meantime, it’s certainly exciting each time a new area is opened up and more electric robotaxis hit the road.

In case you have forgotten where Zoox is in operation, the company informs us: “Atlanta marks our newest testing market for the robotaxi. This is in addition to testing in Austin and Miami, our public service in Las Vegas, and our Zoox Explorers early rider program in San Francisco.”

Also of note is the fact that Zoox didn’t just decide last month to go to Atlanta and rush into the market. It has been laying the groundwork for this launch for about a year and a half in the city. “We started operations in Atlanta in the Spring of 2025, using our testing fleet to map and learn about local driving behaviors, weather patterns, and the city infrastructure. Since then, we have been steadily expanding our driving capabilities, including beginning autonomous driving, and growing our geofence, fleet size, and team to prepare for this next stage of testing.” Zoox explains further how this is central to how Zoox operates:

“Zoox has always been thoughtful and measured in our approach to rolling out autonomous technology at every level. Before we even hit the road and begin driving with our testing fleet in any capacity, we first engage with local and state officials and regulators. Our philosophy is ‘no surprises’ as we lay the foundations for future service markets.

“Along with engaging with local and state officials and regulators, we also love partnering with the community. Workforce development starts long before a first job. That’s why we’re partnering with @Promise Center to help local youth learn, grow, and prepare for their futures in a safe, supportive environment. This partnership reflects our commitment to the Atlanta community. We’re excited to continue investing in the next generation and the future of this city.”

Circling back to Atlanta and why the company has made that one of the first cities for its robotaxi deployment, Zoox adds the following: “Atlanta is a dynamic, vibrant city. Known as the ‘Silicon Valley of the South,’ it boasts one of the largest ride-hailing markets in the United States. Atlanta’s dense, urban layout creates strong demand for efficient transportation solutions, which is where on-demand autonomous ride-hailing comes in. It also has a growing population, and demand like this is exactly why we’re excited to bring Zoox to Atlantans.”

Lastly, as I also highlighted in my article last night about Zoox expanding in Las Vegas, one key thing Zoox is proud of and argues sets it apart from the competition is how vertically integrated its robotaxi business is and how useful the design of its vehicle is for its purpose. Here’s more: “While Atlanta has become a hub for autonomous testing, Zoox continues to stand apart from other companies. Unlike the retrofitted solutions currently on the road, our robotaxi was built from the ground up for fully autonomous ride-hailing. It has no steering wheel or driver’s seat, instead featuring spacious, carriage-style seating for up to four passengers. This design layout allows us to offer Zoox passengers more than just a ride; we are providing a private space where riders can socialize, relax, and reclaim their time. […]

“Zoox owns, operates, and assembles its vehicles, and is the only company currently deploying a fully driverless, purpose-built robotaxi on public roads in the U.S.

“We see promise in bringing our robotaxi service to Atlanta, and look forward to offering Atlantans this unique and private space to socialize, rock out, and create their own experience while being transported to their destination.”

You can learn more on the Zoox website or the Zoox app.

According to the listing, it was repainted in the same color in 1982, and as such, this is one seriously dashing car. This is more of a stylish cruiser than a drag strip dominator, and honestly, I think it's better for it. Whoever ends up winning this immaculate fastback will be the proud owner of a sparkling piece of American automotive history.

#5638. Study Pinpoints States with Steepest Warming Trends Since 1980

The findings indicate where adaptive measures are needed most around the United States.

Global warming, the observed increase in the Earth’s average global surface temperature since preindustrial (1850-1900) times, currently stands at around 1.63 degrees Celsius. While this number is expected to continue to rise, local temperatures will not go up uniformly around the world. In regions where warming trends are most pronounced, local adaptation and resilience measures will be especially critical to minimizing risks to ecosystems, agricultural productivity, the built environment, human health, and economic well-being.

To that end, a new open-access study in the journal Scientific Data identifies the highest-risk regions for warming within the United States. Using data from well-known, high-resolution climate and weather datasets (MERRA2 and ERA5) covering the years 1980-2022, researchers at the MIT Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy (CS3) report global warming-attributed trends in monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature for every U.S. state.

The study finds that Alaska, Utah, New Mexico, Colorado, and Nevada have experienced the strongest average warming trends; the lowest occurred in Hawaii, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Arkansas. Across the country, warming trends were most pronounced during the summer and fall, particularly in September and November. Alaska has the highest historical maximum daily temperature warming (an average of 2.5 C of monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature increase per degree of global warming), while Hawaii has the lowest average historical warming, at 0.8 C.

The authors expect that barring unforeseen local anomalies, these state-by-state temperature trends will continue unabated as ongoing global emissions from human activities continue to raise the average global temperature.

“Based on these results, we encourage decision-makers to assess states that have undergone the steepest increases in maximum and minimum daily temperatures, and identify where continued trends would indicate a rapid progression toward thresholds beyond which natural and managed resources, ecosystems, and infrastructure can function safely,” says MIT CS3 Deputy Director C. Adam Schlosser, a co-author of the study. “In such cases, triaging and adaptive measures would take a high priority. By directing resources to where they are needed most, state and regional planners could significantly reduce climate-related physical and financial risks.”

Unlike previous efforts to report temperature trends across the United States, this study aggregates average maximum, minimum, and mean daily temperature data at the state level for each month of the year, providing actionable information for planners in government, industry, and civil society.

By Mark Dwortzan | Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy, MIT

#5637. Bon Secours Mercy Health bumps up offer for majority stake in Surgery Partners to $6B valuation

Bon Secours Mercy Health bumps up offer for majority stake in Surgery Partners to $6B valuation" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Bon Secours Mercy Health bumped the price tag on its pending transaction to acquire a majority share in healthcare services company Surgery Partners in response to an unsolicited offer the short-stay surgical platform received from a third party, the organizations shared this week.

The transaction now values the acquiree at $6 billion, or $25 per share, up from the initial $5.7 billion and $23.50 per share (see that story below). Additionally, the parties agreed to an additional $1.61 per share in ticking fees if the deal doesn't close by March 1, 2027.

The companies' announcement does not name the third party, which offered $28 per share in a Nov. 3 proposal. A report from Bloomberg, citing an unnamed source, names UnitedHealth as the extra bidder whose offer was rejected over concerns about deal complexity and ability to close.

Surgery Partners’ business platform includes ambulatory surgery centers, surgical hospitals and about 5,000 affiliated physicians spanning 30 states. It reported $3.31 billion in revenue during 2025 and $0.47 adjusted earnings per share.

Affiliates of Bain Capital Private Equity currently control about 39% of Surgery Partners. Under the current deal, Bain would roll over its shares while the remainder would be acquired by a Bon Secours affiliate, HealthSpan Partners.

Bon Secours Mercy Health is acquiring a majority share in healthcare services company Surgery Partners in a take-private deal valuing the acquiree at $5.7 billion, the organizations announced Monday morning.

The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of next year, pending approvals, and with over 200 locations in tow, would help the major nonprofit health system create “one of the country’s largest outpatient surgical care platforms,” they said.

“As healthcare continues to evolve, it is important to grow in ways that allow us to serve more people, in more communities and through a broader range of care settings,” John M. Starcher, Jr., president and CEO of Bon Secours Mercy Health, said in the announcement. “Our relationship with Surgery Partners represents an important step toward advancing that commitment."

Currently, affiliates of Bain Capital Private Equity control about 39% of the public Surgery Partners. Under the terms of the deal, Bain Capital would retain and roll over those shares, while HealthSpan Partners, an affiliate of Bon Secours, would purchase the remainder with cash at $23.50 per share.

Surgery Partners’ short-stay surgical platform includes ambulatory surgery centers, surgical hospitals and about 5,000 affiliated physicians spanning 30 states. It reported $3.31 billion in revenue during 2025 and $0.47 adjusted earnings per share.

The company has been public since 2015, with a 2017 merger making it the largest standalone, independent surgical facilities operator at the time. Bain Capital made an offer in January 2025 to fully acquire the shares it didn’t own for $25.75 apiece (roughly $6.7 billion enterprise valuation), though that offer was rejected a few months later.

Surgery Partners has also been slimming down some of its acute care holdings in recent months, a strategic move its leadership said would better position the company as a purely short-stay surgical provider while limiting its exposure to Medicaid.

“We believe this transaction represents the best path forward for Surgery Partners, delivering an attractive all-cash premium to our shareholders while creating lasting benefits for our patients, physicians and other stakeholders,” Surgery Partners CEO Eric Evans said Monday.

Bon Secours Mercy Health is a Catholic nonprofit with 47 hospitals, more than 1,200 care sites and nearly 60,000 employees. It reported just shy of $14 billion in total operating revenue through 2025, as well as $324 million of recurring operating income (2.3% recurring operating margin) and a $1.1 billion bottom line. Of note, its holdings include 41% ownership in revenue cycle management company Ensemble Health Partners, for which a summer strategic recapitalization transaction with a new private equity investor injected $670.8 million in cash into the system, per recent financial statements.

Bon Secours’ HealthSpan Partners is financing the Surgery Partners purchase with a combination of cash on hand and newly secured debt. Upon closing, the parties plan to keep Surgery Partners’ operations, brand and headquarters in place, while also keeping the business as a secular organization.

Strategically, the deal is evidence of large health systems’ growing investments in ambulatory care networks, where many expect to see rising demand as consumers prioritize lower-cost care settings. Healthcare executives have bluntly described these investments as a “top priority,” particularly as regulatory and policy activity such as the wind-down of Medicare’s inpatient-only list pushes care outside of the hospital.

“As more care moves beyond the hospital setting, patients are looking for high-quality care that fits more seamlessly into their lives,” Wael Haidar, M.D., Bon Secours Mercy Health’s president of clinical operations, said in the announcement. “Surgery Partners understands that care should be designed around the needs of patients, and that approach aligns closely with our mission. Together, we have an opportunity to expand access to high-quality outpatient care while supporting physicians and helping patients receive the right care, in the right setting, at the right time.”

The most apparent analogue for Bon Secours’ deal comes from Ascension, an even larger Catholic nonprofit, which closed a $3.9 billion deal over the summer to acquire AMSURG, an ambulatory surgery management services company with over 300 locations. Ascension CEO Eduardo Conrado has described that deal as both a means to flesh out his system’s existing markets—improving overall volumes and allowing hospitals to focus on high-complexity patients—and a way to strike new business partnerships with other local health systems in markets beyond its prior footprint.

#5636. Every Car Brand That's Made A V10-Powered Sedan

With downsizing being a priority today, thanks chiefly to ever-stricter emissions regulations, a good number of supercars are being sold with six-cylinder engines. In fact, you could even argue that some four-cylinder cars could qualify as supercars today. However, less than a decade earlier, we had a trio of V10-powered sedans sitting in mainstream automaker showrooms — crazy, yet that was the reality of the '00s super-sedan market. BMW dropped a 5.0-liter V10 mill into an otherwise fairly regular-looking 5 Series, Audi furnished its S- and RS-badged sedans with a 5.2-liter lump, and Volkswagen went so far as to develop a diesel-powered V10 for its Bentley-based luxobarge that hardly anyone even remembers existed.

This article shines a light on those fascinating 10-cylinder sedans, zeroing in on the prices, performance specs, and general absurdity each brought to the table. We'll also take a look at how much each example commands today, and what litany of issues typically drain the wallet of anyone foolish enough to take one on. While those models are listed below in chronological order of release, we've also included a brief look at a pair of show-stopping V10-powered sedan concepts that sadly never saw the light of day. One was silenced by a shift in direction, while another found itself permanently postponed by the hands of the '08 financial crisis.

The Volkswagen Phaeton was the first 10-cylinder sedan to break onto the market. It arrived in 2003, designed to elevate Volkswagen's position in the car industry, and Ferdinand Piëch and his team equipped it with all the vital tools to do so. Air suspension, immensely comfortable leather seats, a ridiculously complex A/C system, and a whole host of cool engine options.

The base model came with Volkswagen's weird VR6, which sounds ace and delivers a respectable punch of power — as does the optional 4.2-liter V8. A 3.0-liter direct-injection turbodiesel (TDI) was available in other markets, but for the big spenders, Volkswagen offered both a 6.0-liter W12 and a 4.9-liter V10 TDI. The latter produced 313 horsepower alongside 553 pound-feet of torque – ample for a German luxury sedan at the time.

It wasn't an option that made it to the U.S. market. Instead, Americans received the V8 and W12. Across the pond in the U.K., though, the V10 Phaeton went on sale in early 2003 with a sticker of £57,840, or the equivalent of $95,574 back then. Adjusted for inflation, that comes out to about $175,000 today. Depreciation has really played its part with this forgotten flagship, though, and as a result, prices rarely top £10,000 ($13,480) today. Meanwhile, its W12-powered counterparts regularly trade hands for around $15,000 to $20,000 in the U.S., depending on mileage.

As for what to watch out for, the consensus is just about everything. There was little room in the engine bay, so owners detail that some jobs — like turbocharger replacement — are an engine-out ordeal. That makes work both labor-intensive and not DIY-friendly, and big bills make what is essentially a fancy Passat quite difficult to justify.

It was the E60-generation M5 that next appeared on the 10-cylinder sedan scene, debuting as a 2005 model year. Unlike the Phaeton, which was sold as a comfort-first luxury car, the E60 M5 was first and foremost a performance car. It famously takes power from the naturally aspirated S85 5.0-liter V10, which delivers 500 hp alongside 384 lb-ft of torque. A high compression ratio of 12:1 ensured the M5 meets its 100-hp-per-liter target, and it revs all the way to 8,250 rpm, too. The brilliance of this design was rewarded with the coveted International Engine of the Year Award in both '05 and '06, and it's an engine that still attracts much enthusiast attention 20-plus years later.

When new, buyers would have had to fork out $84,895 for one of these V10-powered super-sedans, and while they have indeed depreciated quite heavily over the last two decades, prices are once again on the move. Classic.com shows $25,555 as the average price paid for SMG-equipped examples, while six-speed manual cars command a significant premium at $45,127. That premium comes down to collectors cherishing the stick-shift involvement, but also ostensibly to the fact that SMG transmissions are so troublesome and expensive to repair — hydraulic pump failures are regular and can easily set owners back thousands of dollars to correct. Aside from SMG woes, the V10 itself is particularly trouble-prone, with its oil pump, throttle body actuators, and rod bearings being known weak spots.

Volkswagen and BMW put their V10 engines into multiple cars, but only ever into a single sedan. Audi outdid them both combined, placing V10s under the hood of C6-generation S6 and RS6 models, in addition to the D3-era S8. The V10-powered S6 arrived in the U.S. as a 2007 model year, as did the S8, while the C6 RS6 sadly avoided the U.S. market altogether.

In these S6 and S8 sedans, torque sat at 398 lb-ft, although the S8 delivered a touch more horsepower: 450 hp compared to the S6's 435. However, when it comes to sheer performance, the forbidden-fruit RS model is the real star of the show. While the S-badged cars featured a naturally aspirated 5.2-liter V10, the RS6 used a 5.0-liter V10 aided by a pair of turbochargers. At the time of its 2008 model-year debut, it was the most powerful production Audi car of all time, kicking out 579 hp and 479 lb-ft.

When shiny and new, buyers were paying £76,160 for an RS6 Sedan, or the equivalent of about $150,000 back then, which would amount to $239,440 today. We drove the latest RS6 Avant, which cost $122,995, so perhaps the C6-era car was a little expensive, but applying financial logic to a twin-turbocharged 10-cylinder probably isn't the best way to look at such a car.

Like the others, these cars have depreciated massively. A simple oil pump seal often necessitates a multi-thousand-dollar engine-out job on the RS6, and that pretty much sets the precedent for any 10-cylinder sedan ownership experience. Still, the fact that used U.S.-market S6 and S8 models can be secured for below $10,000 with reasonable mileage today at least leaves the deep-pocketed among us plenty of cash left over for maintenance.

That concludes our list of V10-powered sedans that made production, and it might seem remarkable that $25,000 is enough to find yourself in a seat in any of them. What's interesting, though, is that a different pair of automakers also looked to produce their own 10-cylinder sedans in the '00s, but sadly never made it all the way.

First up was Ford. The Blue Oval brand released its startling 427 Concept in 2003, and it was designed to recapture the glory of America's traditional and luxurious four-door sedan. Motivating the sharp concept was a modular V10, which boasted a full 427 cubic inches of displacement plus 590 hp and 509 lb-ft of torque — all of which was directed toward the rear wheels. In the end, it remained just a concept, as Ford instead shifted its attention toward other performance models, such as the 2005 Ford GT and the S-197 Mustang.

The other concept worth shining a light on is the 2008 Lamborghini Estoque. It was sort of the Urus before the Urus, but it wasn't an SUV but rather a Lamborghini designed around daily life — think commutes and school drop-offs, rather than cross-country road trips and tire-shredding track days. It was set to be powered by a variant of the Gallardo V10. Buyers could have expected somewhere in the region of 500 horsepower, but it was never to be. With the global recession underway, and Lamborghini ready to explore a more practical model, the Estoque was no longer the flavor of the month. Instead, the Urus would have its day, but we can still reminisce about what could have been.

#5635. No Surprises Act IDR claims cost employer plans an additional $8.4B last year, study finds

No Surprises Act IDR claims cost employer plans an additional $8.4B last year, study finds" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The No Surprises Act's independent dispute resolution process cost employer plans $8.39 billion in 2025, according to a new analysis.

Researchers at the Employee Benefit Research Institute combed federal IDR data and found that these additional costs equal about 63 cents per $100 spent by employer-based insurance plans. The total includes $4.73 billion in costs incurred in the first half of the year as well as $3.66 billion in the second half of 2025.

Even when EBRI analysts used different thresholds to exclude outlier awards, such as costs that were unusually high, they still landed on an estimate of at least $8.02 billion, per the study.

The researchers note that this data doesn't necessarily paint the full picture, as it only encompasses cases that proceeded to IDR. The study doesn't include information on claims that were settled outside of arbitration, administrative costs, any changes in networks or provider rates or the cost associated with patient protections.

The study calculates additional cost by taking the IDR award amounts and subtracting the plan's initial payment and any cost-sharing from the patient.

"These new data provide a clearer picture of what health plans owe for out-of-network services beyond their initial payments, after accounting for patient cost sharing,” said Paul Fronstin, Ph.D., director of Health Benefits Research at EBRI, in the announcement. “Separating those amounts from arbitration awards allows us to measure additional plan obligations more directly."

The study also doesn't project the impact of IDR on premiums, and the researchers said that having greater insight into the administrative expenses and other ancillary costs would be necessary to understand how the No Surprises Act's processes may impact patients' costs directly.

The IDR processes have gained increasing scrutiny from health plans and plan sponsors as the number of disputes, and their associated payouts, rise. When a claim reaches the arbitration phase, the results overwhelming favor providers, as they won in 85% of disputes last year.

An analysis from Georgetown University, released in August, estimated that total costs associated with IDR reached $22 billion in 2025. There were 2.6 million disputes initiated in 2025; by comparison, federal estimates projected about 22,000 cases annually reaching the arbitration phase.

Providers have pushed back on criticism of IDR, arguing that the root cause is payers undercutting them during the opening negotiation phase by setting low qualifying payment amounts for claims.

#5634. AI Businesses Still Bleeding Billions

AI is fun and cool when it creates useful things for you or answers tough questions quickly and well (let’s not focus on AI slop and false claims at the moment), but that doesn’t mean AI businesses are financially sustainable or sensible. AI companies are still heavily subsidizing their broad use, with the benefits for them being growing user bases and sky-high valuations. These companies are burning billions of dollars each quarter on the hype and promise that they will rule the world one day (quite literally).

OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, reported this week that it had $10.9 billion in operating losses last quarter. That’s up from $10.1 billion in operating losses in the second quarter.

One might think that means not a lot changed, and certainly nothing positive. However, the company’s revenue was actually up by 50%! So, even with a huge boost in revenue, gigantic losses grew! Furthermore, the company was apparently even using a tool of “last resort” here.

OpenAI started running ads in ChatGPT, something that the company was adamantly trying to avoid. CEO Sam Altman previously called the proposal to run ads “unsettling” and claimed that the company would only go that route as a matter of “last resort.” Well, it seems the company has reached that point of last resort. And that can’t be a good thing, right? Considering that OpenAI is still losing billions of dollars a quarter, it’s even more concerning. What comes after a “last resort” effort to turn finances around?

Frankly, I wish we could spend billions of dollars a quarter to make CleanTechnica into a behemoth of a media organization! That would be amazing — imagine all of the stuff we could do! But what are the chances we’d be losing billions of dollars a quarter in doing so? And how long could we operate like that before external sources of funding stopped covering the bill?

As we know, OpenAI is one of the “leaders” of the AI industry. If it is struggling like this, who isn’t, and what does that mean for the industry overall and where it’s headed?

The one big player that has been raking in the dough in the midst of this enormous AI craze is NVIDIA, and look at what’s now happening there! Where are things going to go with that company?

“The news comes not long after controversy over how OpenAI was projecting its earnings. In October, the company reported an annualized revenue, an estimate of how much money it will earn over a year, of about $50 billion — which was $20 billion short of what it told investors only a month before,” Futurism adds. “The discrepancy was taken as an admission that the business models of AI companies weren’t as robust as their leadership was making them out to be, fueling speculation of an impending bubble.”

Why can’t the leaders of these companies just ask their chatbots how to turn a profit and implement their answers? Well, one of the answers might have been regulatory capture and blocking others from entering the market, but that dream may now be out the window. In my humble opinion, 2027 could be a very interesting year for AI companies, and that might involve a big popping noise.

#5633. Injectable Nanobody Wins FDA Approval for Myasthenia Gravis

— Gefurulimab joins other approved C5 inhibitors

The FDA on Friday approved injectable gefurulimab (Klygefa), a dual-binding nanobody that blocks complement component 5 (C5) activation, to treat generalized myasthenia gravis in adults who are anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody positive.

The approval comes in the wake of the phase III PREVAIL trial, which randomized 260 adults with anti-AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis to receive weekly self-administered subcutaneous gefurulimab or placebo for 26 weeks. The trial met the primary endpoint, showing an improvement in scores on the Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living (MG-ADL) scale versus placebo at week 28, with a treatment difference of -1.6 points.

MG-ADL scores range 0-24 points; improvements emerged in week 1 and continued through week 26. Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis scores -- a key secondary endpoint -- also improved by week 4 compared with placebo, and improvement was sustained throughout the study.

The drug is available only through a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) program. The drug carries a boxed warning for serious and life-threatening infections caused by Neisseria meningitidis. Three other C5 inhibitors have been approved by the FDA for myasthenia gravis: eculizumab (Soliris), ravulizumab (Ultomiris), and zilucoplan (Zilbrysq). All carry a similar warning, and patients are required to comply with recommendations for meningococcal vaccinations.

In PREVAIL, the percentage of participants with treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) was similar between the gefurulimab and placebo groups. Most TEAEs were mild to moderate (grade 1 or 2).

In the gefurulimab group, the most common TEAEs were injection site reactions (9.9%), headache (9.9%), and back pain (7.6%). Twelve people treated with gefurulimab had serious adverse events. One death occurred, which was not considered to be related to treatment.

Gefurulimab binds to serum albumin to provide an extended half-life, allowing once-weekly dosing. "The safety profile was in line with earlier studies of C5 inhibitors in generalized myasthenia gravis," observed Christiane Schneider-Gold, MD, and Ralf Gold, MD, both of Ruhr University Bochum in Germany, in a JAMA Neurology editorial earlier this year. "In addition, no unexpected safety concerns were identified in patients recruited across 20 countries," they wrote.

"Despite rather well-tolerated subcutaneous application, it remains an interesting matter which position gefurulimab will eventually gain in the continuously evolving treatment landscape in generalized myasthenia gravis and among the group of complement inhibitors," Schneider-Gold and Gold noted.

Data from the open-label extension of PREVAIL recently showed that gefurulimab sustained functional benefits through 52 weeks.

In September, the European Medicines Agency's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use recommended gefurulimab for EU approval.

#5632. What A Road Sign With A Black 'Y' Means (And Other Letters, Too)

We have covered all manner of weird road signs on Jalopnik before, including some seriously goofy ones. While oddities from around the globe are fun to explore and explain, it is a little more relevant to touch on road signs that crop up on U.S. soil. Some of these will no doubt be familiar, but others may not, so there is good reason to delve into them and provide a quick explainer. The black "Y" sign was the one that initially piqued our interest, which, by the way, highlights that a Y-shaped intersection is to be found up ahead. That led us to look at other weird letter- and symbol-focused road signs drivers may come across.

The obvious candidates are "P" for parking areas and "H" that marks hospitals, which are universally understood, but throughout this article, we will also explore what those weird "T" or upturned "U" signs mean, in addition to winding "S" and plus-symbol signs. That includes where drivers are most likely to find them and how best to react when they do. Listed in no particular order, here are our picks of eight letter- or symbol-focused road signs that we thought are worth exploring in a bit more detail.

As already explained briefly above, a sign that depicts a capitalized "Y" is there to let drivers know of a Y-shaped three-way intersection or a forked road ahead. The sign will typically be a diamond shape with a yellow background, which means it's a simple warning sign alerting drivers that the road splits. The choices of where to go are obvious — either left or right — but what might be less obvious is how the right of way is determined in a three-way intersection that isn't controlled by any other signs.

The general rule is that drivers must yield to the car on the right. Then there's always the first-to-arrive rule, which works as you would intend — the first to arrive at the split goes first. Of course, some drivers will assume right of way when it is not deserved, or perhaps they just do not see the other car(s). In such instances, it's best to yield to the other vehicle even if you believe you should have the right of way to ensure everyone gets past the intersection without incident.

When a road splits like this, it pays to be especially cautious. Drivers may attempt to dart from one lane to the next when correcting a last-minute wrong decision, plus motorbikes or cyclists could be hiding in your blind spots, so try to ensure you have sufficient space around you if possible. The NHTSA highlights that roughly one third of all traffic fatalities occur at signposted intersections, so doubling down on cautiousness here is never a bad idea, no matter how simple it may first appear.

Surprise surprise, the letter "T" on a road sign warns of a T-shaped intersection — we would hope that you managed to work that one out. The road you are traveling on is about to end and merge with another. Once again, this is a classic warning sign finished in a yellow and black colorway, on a diamond-shaped sign that lets drivers know something's coming up and they will have to act accordingly.

In this instance, drivers must yield to traffic on the intersecting road — they don't have the right of way here — before heading either left or right. There will usually be a stop or yield sign prior to the intersection itself, and to avoid any frustrating bumps with other drivers making late decisions, it's best to get into the required lane early rather than last-minute. Thankfully, of the deadliest intersections on U.S. roads, not many are T-shaped, but the same rules as above apply here. Give yourself space, keep an eye on your blind spots, and don't rush. Oh, and don't forget to use your turn signals either, even if you are in a dedicated turn lane.

Again, we won't be handing out prizes to anyone who is able to correctly guess this one. A cross or "plus" symbol indicates that a crossroad is coming up, and just like the other aforementioned sign, this too will be depicted on a black and yellow diamond-shaped warning sign. Here, traffic can and likely will be coming from all directions, so it's imperative to take the time that's needed and approach it with care. Be aware that drivers on the opposite leg might try to cross ahead of you as you pull out, and be sure to check traffic from both left and right directions. As always, make sure to follow the instructions depicted on any regulatory signs posted in your direction, as these might detail give-way instructions.

There is a good case to make here in favor of the roundabout. In many ways, it is a far better design than the traditional intersection, with fewer conflict points, no left-turns across the flow of traffic, and lower speeds. Roundabouts might seem perplexing to some, but according to data from the Federal Highway Administration, they have been proven to reduce injury and fatal crashes by 76% and 90%, respectively, plus they are far more time-efficient than traffic signals, so perhaps road users ought to just get used to them.

OK, that's not strictly true. This sign, which isn't an "S" at all — it's just a winding arrow — signifies that a winding road is up around. In other words, the natural habitat for a Miata owner who's looking for some engaging roads to make the most of their drop-top weekend car. Of course, the sign isn't actually there to tell drivers that the road is a great place to go hooning. Instead, it lets them know the road ahead has several curves one after another and that they should approach that section of road with some caution.

In fact, these "S" signs will frequently be accompanied by another advisory speed sign that suggests the maximum safe speed for the section. Drivers would be wise to pay attention to these speeds, as around 25% of all fatal road incidents happen on a curved section of road, with common causes being cars either drifting off into trees, rocks, or other fixed objects, or indeed drifting across the center of the road and causing a head-on collision with other traffic.

Anyone who can't figure this one out should probably start taking notes here. An upturned U-shaped arrow crossed out in red, of course, means that U-turns are not permitted. Drivers should continue on, take a left or right turn if available, and find another suitable route. Exceptions will not be made for those in classic red-and-white Gran Torinos.

This is the first sign featured on our list that strays from that typical yellow and black warning sign colorway. Instead, this is a rectangular regulatory sign with a white background. These signs can crop up just about anywhere, but they can commonly be spotted in business districts, on narrow streets, or busier stretches of the nation's roads, such as on multi-lane highways and freeways.

For those who may question the legality of U-turns when this sign isn't present, drivers can usually perform such a move in these circumstances: They should be in the leftmost or center-left lane, signalling their intention, and keeping an eye out for traffic as per any other manoeuvre.

A sideways "T" sign indicates that a side road is coming up. Depending on which way the T is oriented, the sign highlights whether the side road is on the right or the left. If the sign instead looks like an F or an E, but with an extended top or bottom, this means that two side roads are coming up on the right-hand side.

Specifically, this sign will appear when the side roads on the right are particularly close to one another. The hazard this poses to drivers on the major road is quite obvious; they should be wary of traffic entering from the right, and should be prepared to slow down. The sign itself is a typical diamond-shaped yellow-and-black warning sign, which does not indicate right of way. Typically, those on the major road will have the right of way, while those on the indicated side roads will have to yield to traffic on the major road.

The sign for a roundabout shows three arrows forming a circle, and once again, it will be a yellow-and-black diamond-shaped warning sign. Roundabouts always run in a counter-clockwise direction in North America. They can have numerous lanes and are an alternative to crossroads. Here, the right of way rules are simple and uniform: Drivers must always give way to traffic on the left — in other words, the cars that are already on the roundabout.

Getting the right lane is crucial for avoiding accidents; the leftmost lane is used for turning left, whereas the rightmost lanes are used for turning right, and both can be used for going straight on. These are the rules on multi-lane roundabouts unless signposted otherwise — this way, traffic in either lane does not cross unnecessarily.

As for whether drivers need to use turn signals on a roundabout or not, the answer is yes. It's never a bad idea to let other drivers know where you are going; even if you are comfortable in your own abilities to get across safely, it's best practice to help other motorists out by indicating to them your next intended move.

#5630. Texas AG narrows lawsuit against Epic, dropping claims over parental access settings

Texas AG narrows lawsuit against Epic, dropping claims over parental access settings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Texas is dropping a part of its lawsuit against Epic Systems, specifically the claims about how the company's software handles parental access to a child's electronic health records.

In December, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed a lawsuit against Epic, alleging that the health tech company monopolizes the electronic health record market and cements its dominance in the market through an "anticompetitive playbook."

The lawsuit, filed in Tarrant County District Court, also accused the company of engaging in deceptive practices that restrict parental access to their minor children’s medical records. On Tuesday, the Texas AG's office filed a notice of partial non-suit indicating it was dropping the deceptive practices claims against Epic.

The notice of partial non-suit states that the decision was made "in light of Epic’s recent changes to its software."

In previous statements, an Epic spokesperson said the company "does not determine parental access to children’s medical records."

"Decisions about parental access to children’s medical records are made by doctors and health systems, not by Epic," the spokesperson said.

The state is still moving forward with its antitrust claims under the Texas Free Enterprise and Antitrust Act. The Texas Attorney General's office alleges Epic "uses a wide range of exclusionary tactics to prevent potential competition from its partners, customers and even its own employees." According to the suit, these anticompetitive practices harm Texas hospitals and Texas patients by raising costs and blocking innovative technologies.

In the lawsuit, Paxton alleged that Epic "exploits its control" over patient medical records to automatically hide children’s medication lists, treatment notes and provider messages from parents when their child reaches 12 years old. Texas alleged that Epic’s default proxy-access configurations impede parents’ ability to see their children’s health information.

"These deceptive practices undermine the fundamental right of parents to direct their children’s healthcare" and violate Texas law, which grants parents complete and unrestricted access to their children’s medical records, the attorney general's office said in the lawsuit.

In a statement issued in December, Paxton referred to Epic as a "woke corporation" and stated that Epic's default proxy-access configurations "undermine the sacred rights of parents to protect and oversee their kids’ medical well-being."

In a statement provided to Fierce Healthcare on Wednesday, an Epic spokesperson said the Texas lawsuit includes "significant inaccuracies, including claims about MyChart's customer proxy settings."

"The state filed a voluntary dismissal of those claims on Tuesday. Ken Paxton's office requested that we change our customers' system settings. We said no because those decisions should be made by doctors and health systems and not by Epic. The lawsuit followed. The State should dismiss the remaining claims," the Epic spokesperson said.

In a Jan. 20 filing in Tarrant County District Court, the electronic health record giant said it makes "highly configurable software so that its customers, healthcare organizations across all fifty states, can determine what workflows and functionalities are needed to achieve their own compliance obligations—including with respect to parental access rights to medical records."

"What might be compliant in Texas might not be compliant in another state and vice versa, and those laws may change from time to time, as the law just did roughly four months ago in Texas. Configurability helps customers bridge that gap," the company wrote in its filing.

Epic said it would not "unilaterally go into each of its customers’ systems to change their individualized settings."

Epic also argued, in its court filing, that the state failed to produce facts or legitimate legal bases to support any of its claims. "When Epic asked the State to identify any Epic customers it claimed were not in compliance with the new law, the State did not identify a single Epic customer. What appears to be going on here is that the State has decided to target Epic over a politicized issue regarding proxy access that Epic does not belong in the middle of. The State confirms as much in its press release, calling Epic a 'woke corporation' that supposedly 'undermine[s]' parents’ rights," Epic wrote in its answer to the lawsuit.

In its Answer and Affirmative Defenses, Epic said that the state's antitrust claims against it are pre-textual and baseless. Epic denied Paxton's allegations of anticompetitive behavior, citing a lack of evidence and factual flaws in the lawsuit.

The case will carry over into a changing political landscape in Texas. Paxton, who launched the lawsuit, is leaving the Texas attorney general's office after more than a decade, after his unsuccessful bid for the U.S. Senate. Democrat Nathan Johnson defeated Republican Mayes Middleton in the Nov. 3 midterm election, becoming the first Democrat elected Texas attorney general since 1994.

The leadership change could bring a shift in the office's litigation priorities. Paxton's tenure was marked by high-profile legal battles over social and cultural issues, including transgender healthcare and parental rights.

Last year, the Texas Office of the Attorney General secured a settlement with Austin Diagnostic Clinic that required full restoration of parental proxy access for children aged 12 to 17. Paxton has also issued civil investigative demands to other EHR software providers over parental access to minor children's medical records.

The case will also have a new judge. Democrat Katherine Kim defeated Republican incumbent H. Dustin "Dusty" Fillmore III in the race for Tarrant County's 236th Judicial District Court.

#5629. The Crucial Difference Between Flock Cameras And Plate Readers In Other Countries

Stories about Flock cameras and other stalkerish automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) have been a mainstay of American news for the last year or two, and horror stories involving this questionable technology are everywhere. From police using ALPRs to stalk citizens to AI-powered ALPRs flagging innocent auto journalists for stealing vehicles, there's no shortage of evidence that ALPRs are making the world worse. A lot of such stories you see in the news and even here on Jalopnik are about misuse of and issues with ALPRs specifically in the United States, though. While there's certainly some bias toward American news on publications based in the States, it still does raise the question: Are there Flock cameras or equivalents in other countries? And if so, do they cause the same volume of issues?

The answer is an interesting one. First, yes, ALPRs do exist outside of the United States, though the technology is often called automatic number plate recognition, or ANPR, due to regional differences in how license plates are referred to. Nearly 100 countries use this technology to track automobile movement and other data. However, Flock cameras themselves aren't nearly as prevalent outside the United States. In fact, the big difference between the implementation of license plate recognition technology in the U.S. and abroad is in who owns it and how the data collected is managed.

See, Flock Safety and Axon, two of the biggest promulgators of ALPR tech in the States, are privately operated companies that contract their services out to the state via entities like police departments and city councils. In other countries, and European countries in particular, ALPRs are typically owned, deployed, and operated by the state itself, rather than subcontracted through private companies. This distinction might just make all the difference.

If you're skeptical that a state-owned surveillance network is different than a privately owned, state-sponsored surveillance, well, you know, that's fair. But there are indeed some notable differences between how this technology is treated in the U.S. and how it's used abroad.

The rest of the world is certainly no stranger to surveillance. For example, the UK has a massive network of CCTV cameras that leave urban areas like London heavily monitored at all times, and they're now employing AI to level up their surveillance efforts, too. AI-powered surveillance is also rapidly ramping up in China, Brazil, and Australia.

Whether these networks are installed and operated by governments or private entities, the fact is that there's room for abuse by those with access to the data. However, in some other locations, it's easier for governments to regulate and oversee how the data is used. For example, European ALPR data is protected by the region's General Data Protection Regulation, which is way more than we have here in the ALPR Wild West.

In the U.S., Flock data from one municipality can be accessed by basically anyone in other areas with a Flock contract, and hackers who pulled a Flock camera apart showed that it's pretty easy to get the stored data even without a contract. Some police officers have even been caught accessing Flock data after leaving the force, according to the Washington Post. When this happens, finding accountability can be hard. ALPRs owned and run by the state directly at least have clear channels for voicing dissent, though it may also be true that they're more entrenched and harder to remove.

#5627. Fabric Molds Could Bring Material-Saving Concrete Beams Within Reach

MIT engineers cast a concrete beam using a sewn fabric mold with one-third the amount of concrete and half as much steel as a conventional beam.

Topology optimization is a computer design method that can help engineers design beams using reduced amounts of concrete and steel. But those intricate shapes produced from the tool are often too complex or expensive to pour into conventional rigid molds. The few that have been built have mostly relied on specialized equipment, such as concrete 3D printers or machine-carved molds, equipment that is out of reach in regions where new construction is expected to grow.

Now, MIT engineers have shown that highly efficient beams can be cast in something more accessible: sewn fabric. In a paper published in the Journal of Building Engineering, the team designed and built a 3-meter (about 10-foot) test beam using fabric molds created through an automated pattern-making process. Compared with a conventional beam designed to carry the same weight, the optimized beam used about one-third as much concrete and half as much steel reinforcement. When tested, its measured response was within about 2 percent of what the team’s computer model predicted.

Fabric formwork, in which concrete is poured into a mold made of textile, has been explored for years to create beams that vary in depth, rather than in rectangular shapes common in construction. But because fabric deforms under the weight of wet concrete, that flexibility has made the final shape hard to predict.

“The key realization was that this flexibility is not just a limitation to manage; with the right computational pattern design, it can become a way to produce optimized structural forms,” says Josephine Carstensen, the Gilbert W. Winslow (1937) Career Development Professor in Civil Engineering and senior author of the study.

Fabric molds can also be inexpensive, lightweight, and fast compared to wood or steel molds. “You could sew a formwork together off site, pack it into a box, and bring it to a job site very easily,” says Jackson Jewett PhD ’25, co-author of the study. “We joke that we are developing the H&M of the construction industry.”

Cement production accounts for roughly 8 percent of human-caused carbon emissions.

“This work addresses concrete’s climate footprint primarily by reducing material demand,” Carstensen says. “Cement production is highly carbon-intensive, so using less concrete is an important part of decarbonizing construction.”

Where new construction happens matters, too. The world’s number of buildings is expected to nearly double by 2050, with about 85 percent of that growth in developing countries, where access to advanced construction equipment is often limited. That is why, Carstensen says, the team focused on an accessible, cost-conscious fabrication approach.

Concrete is strong when compressed, but weak when pulled, so it’s reinforced with steel that can handle the pulling forces. The researchers first mapped a path for the steel reinforcement using a method called graphic statics, which can generate structural designs almost instantly. They used it to shape the steel bar so that it carries an equal share of the weight along its entire length to keep the reinforcement simple enough for builders to make. Topology optimization, which works more slowly but can place material freely, was used to determine where concrete was needed and where material could be removed from areas where it contributes little to the structural performance.

“Both methods are good at different things, so we tried to combine the strengths of both into a single methodology,” says Jewett.

The resulting beam has a top section, narrow angled legs, and a thin bottom section for the steel reinforcement. The team’s automated process translated the 3D beam design into flat fabric pieces that can be cut and sewn into a mold, accounting for how the fabric will deform once concrete is poured in. A simple timber frame supported the finished fabric mold.

For Mark Hellrich SM ’26, the study’s lead author, the main hands-on challenge was getting the concrete mix right. Woven cotton fabric lets water seep through, so a mix that is too runny loses water through the mold. It also presses harder against the fabric, pushing it away from the intended shape.

The team used a moderately wet, sand-rich mix with only small stones, so the concrete could flow through the beam’s narrow, angled legs and thin bottom section without getting stuck. They then packed it in by hand, prodding each layer and tapping and kneading the fabric from the outside.

“This is where the flexibility of the mold becomes an advantage: you can work the concrete through the interconnected passages without a vibrator, which a rigid mold of this shape would need,” says Hellrich. A concrete vibrator is a tool typically used to shake air pockets out of freshly poured concrete in rigid molds.

Once the concrete was in place, the wet fabric revealed the beam’s final shape. “All three beams were free of wrinkles and creases,” says Hellrich. The top surface stayed close to the design, while the main difference was a downward sag along the bottom, with the angled legs folding slightly inward.

To find out how much sewing precision the beam needs, the team built three molds for the same design, made from 36, 56, and 76 fabric pieces. Comparing the 3D scans of the cast beams with the target design, the researchers found that more seams gave finer control over the details, but did not necessarily make the beam’s overall shape more accurate.

“More seams improve local control because they divide the fabric into smaller, more constrained panels. But a more complex pattern also has more pieces to align and more seam length, so small cutting, sewing, and assembly inaccuracies can accumulate across the mold, explains Carstensen.

The 56-piece mold demonstrated the best balance, capturing the important design geometry without the added time, effort, and potential errors associated with the most complex pattern.

The researchers then load-tested one of the beams, gradually stacking 36 water-filled buckets on top of it, up to about 30 percent of its design load to reflect everyday service conditions. Weighted lines hung from the beam’s underside to precise measuring gauges below, tracking how far the beam bent as the load was added and removed. At the beam’s center, the measured deflection — its downward movement under the load — was within about 2 percent of the computer model’s prediction.

The team also compared the cost of a single fabric-formed beam with a conventional one and found that location makes all the difference. In the Global South, where materials tend to cost more relative to labor, all three fabric versions were cheaper, with savings of about 10 to 20 percent. In the Global North, higher labor costs for sewing reversed that advantage, making the fabric versions about 16 to 55 percent more expensive.

The findings suggest that fabric formwork is most promising for custom-shaped concrete components produced as a one-off or in small batches, such as exposed beams, roof or long-span framing, pedestrian structures, and landscape elements. For the repetitive, rectangular beams found in most buildings, conventional reusable molds remain the more economical choice where labor is expensive.

“To get started, a builder would need the digital pattern for the target component, a sewing machine and suitable fabric, and a simple timber support frame,” Carstensen says. “That is a much lower equipment threshold than robotic fabrication, concrete 3D printing, or CNC-milled molds.”

The researchers describe the 3-meter beam as a proof of concept comparable to a short building span. It is also a big step up from the 1.2-meter beam the team built in a previous project, Jewett notes.

Building bigger isn’t just a matter of enlarging the design, Carstensen notes. As a beam gets longer, its own weight and the pressure on the fabric mold change, so a larger beam would need a new design. The next step, Carstensen says, is “to test multiple beams to failure.”

“The nice thing about these optimization methods is they generate structures that look organic,” Jewett says. “Their geometries are clear expressions of how the forces move through the structural system. There is elegance to them. It makes you ask why we don’t design all our structures in this way.”

Joining Carstensen, Jewett, and Hellrich on the paper are co-authors Abhinit Sati, Edward Chien, and Emily Whiting, of Boston University’s Department of Computer Science.

The work was partially supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation.

By Stephanie Martinovich | Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, MIT

#5626. Medical transport platform MedHaul, focused on high-needs patients, raises $4.1M

Medical transport platform MedHaul, focused on high-needs patients, raises $4.1M" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

MedHaul, a platform for coordinating medical transport, has raised $4.1 million in an unnamed round, Fierce Healthcare has learned exclusively.

The strategic round, which brings MedHaul’s total raised to date to $7 million, was led by Black Ops VC, with participation from Pier 70 Ventures, Seae Ventures, Stanford University, 450 Ventures (BCBS of Alabama), LaunchTN and American Cancer Society’s BrightEdge.

The latest capital will be used to expand deeper in oncology, which represents 60% of rides booked on the platform, and to support a forthcoming Epic integration.

Millions of Americans are affected by transportation barriers to care, and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services estimates that these barriers account for a quarter or more of missed clinic appointments. Missed appointments are associated with mortality among patients with chronic conditions and cost the system billions annually, according to one 2017 estimate.

MedHaul is a B2B platform working with providers and payers. Its tech helps providers match patients with medical transport according to acuity and accommodation needs, such as a wheelchair or stretcher. Care teams can use MedHaul to schedule and track transportation, with same-day and advanced bookings available. They can also manage billing, communicate with patients and identify those at greater risk of missing an appointment. MedHaul also rolled out a newer clinical trial product designed to support CROs and pharma clients.

The existing medical transport ecosystem is “very antiquated” and “heavily manual,” MedHaul founder and CEO Erica Plybeah told Fierce Healthcare. Many transport companies are small businesses that are not tech-savvy, or that need business development support. When MedHaul first entered the market, in 2019, some vendors didn’t even have a website or a social media page, Plybeah noted. And manual back-and-forths between care teams and ride providers means it can take upwards of two hours just to book a ride.

MedHaul’s network spans 17 states, primarily serving patients in the cancer, kidney disease, maternal health and behavioral health spaces. It also supports hospital discharges and rural patients. It has about 600 transport companies in its network.

MedHaul has also launched an enterprise platform, designed for large health systems and multi-location practices. Through a partnership with Uber Health, ride share and non-emergency medical transport bookings are available in one place, on the platform. The platform also provides real-time analytics into patient mobility, enabled by AI.

"There are opportunities in healthcare where AI is bridging the gap to solve for unmet needs—and that’s exactly what Erica and her team are doing at MedHaul,” James Norman, co-founder & managing partner at Black Ops VC, said in a statement. The user-friendly interface and focus on high-acuity communities “make MedHaul an attractive investment, and we’re proud to help them scale.”

Plybeah, who grew up in the Deep South with a grandmother who had diabetic and a double-leg amputee, saw how transportation issues affected her access to care. Throughout her career in clinical and research informatics, including at Epic Systems and St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, Plybeah “saw how transportation impacted institutions, when patients don’t show up on time, don’t show up at all, show up at the wrong facility … and it brought me back to being a little girl in the Mississippi Delta.”

Over half of MedHaul’s rides require mobility assistance, and 42% live in rural communities. MedHaul’s riders averaged eight rides per year in 2025.

Patients typically don’t pay anything for the rides booked on MedHaul. Instead, the MedHaul client—a provider or payer, for instance—sponsors the rides, often from an existing medical transport budget. In specialties with high transport volumes, providers may also use a patient’s benefit to find rides.

Same-day rides are available within 30 minutes to an hour, depending on acuity. For higher-acuity patients, a booking can take two to three hours, depending on the complexity of the transport required. MedHaul sees a 97% ride completion rate. Providers using MedHaul have reduced missed appointments by 25% and improved patient appointment timeliness by 52%, the company claims.

MedHaul has long used AI across its business. It has a conversational AI agent for older adults who prefer phone calls to texting. It also leverages AI agents to book rides within seconds for highly complex patients, and offers care teams MedHaul GPT, which they can use to ask questions about their programs and patients.

“We really prioritize good implementation,” Plybeah said, noting that there has been an explosion in digital health point solutions, but implementation is a whole different question. “We want this process to be as easy as possible for the end users.”

The company, which launched in 2019, is a public benefit corporation and a certified B Corp. While it’s still a for-profit business, its structure requires it to pursue a stated public benefit alongside financial returns. “We wanted our mission to extend beyond profit and to attract the right partners, investors, employees and customers who shared that commitment,” Plybeah said. “Our social mission is embedded in how we operate, build technology, serve patients and choose the people and organizations we work with.”

Plybeah is excited that there is more industry awareness of the social determinants of health. In the early MedHaul days, “folks seemed to think of transportation as a separate service,” she said. “And now I am grateful to see that folks are really considering transportation as part of the patient’s care journey, because it is.”
