#5611. Mini Truck Vs. Side-By-Side: What Are The Practical Differences?

You've likely seen those neat little mini trucks from Japan. They're the size of a compact vehicle, but have a bed as long as some full-size pickups. These Kei trucks, as they are called, look like they would be pretty practical for a number of uses.

President Trump was quite smitten with Kei trucks when he saw them in Japan, apparently for the first time, later calling them "really cute." And in a December 2025 Truth Social post, he said that he had "approved" the manufacture of these "tiny" vehicles here. But, as is the case with many of the president's statements, no one is quite sure what that means. Unfortunately, you can't buy a new one for road use in the U.S., but older ones are available thanks to an exception in import laws.

Maybe you're thinking about snagging one of these trucks for your farm, ranch, or construction site and wondering how they compare to those side-by-sides that are made for work. These utility task vehicles (UTVs) also have a bed on the back and are often used to haul small loads around on a worksite. There are several differences. For one thing, you can easily find new UTVs for sale. Their payload and towing capacities are often higher than those of most Kei trucks. They are built more for off-roading, while Kei trucks are built for the street. It really comes down to what your needs are, though.

Kei trucks were not made to meet U.S. safety and environmental standards. The Clean Air Act prohibits importing a vehicle that doesn't meet federal emissions standards unless it's at least 21 years old. Federal law also bans foreign vehicles less than 25 years old that don't meet safety standards.

Newer Kei trucks can be imported only as off-road vehicles, permanently limited to 25 mph. That means if you want one for the road, you're stuck shopping for used Kei trucks that are at least 25 years old. That's not to say they're hard to find. Type "used Kei truck for sale" into Google and you'll see several listings for Kei trucks, as well as businesses that sell them. And the ones we've seen look to be in better shape than the typical 25- or 30-year-old vehicle, on the outside at least.

It's a bit more straightforward with UTVs, or side-by-sides. They are off-road vehicles, so they are perfectly legal to sell brand-new in the U.S. We found 25 Polaris dealerships and at least 30 Honda Powersports dealerships in the state of Florida alone. Of course, there are plenty of used side-by-sides all over the place, as well. Sites like ATV Trader, ATVHunt, and Autotrader all contain several listings.

You're going to get a longer, more versatile bed with a mini truck than you will with a UTV. Anyone can see that just by looking at the two vehicles. Kei truck beds are often over 6 feet long and over 4 feet wide. With the tailgate down, that's big enough to haul a piece of plywood or drywall, with just a little bit hanging over the edge.

The sides of a Kei truck's bed often fold down, allowing for easy loading of a packed pallet by a forklift. The walls are not very high, which makes it easier to load and offload the bed, as well. Beds on UTVs are often much smaller, with the boxes on some models being around 3.5 feet in length and a little over 4 feet in width.

Don't confuse bed size with payload capacity, however. Kei trucks, as regulated by the Japanese government, can carry no more than 771 pounds of cargo. On the other hand, the Polaris Ranger XD 1500 has a box capacity of 1,500 pounds, which is on the high end for UTVs. We should point out, though, that payload capacity is the final word on how much you can load into your vehicle. The total weight of passengers in the cab and cargo in the box should not exceed payload capacity, regardless of box capacity.

Comparing the towing capacities of mini trucks and side-by-sides is tricky because there aren't any official towing capacities published for Kei trucks. Japan's registration calculation caps the total weight of a brakeless trailer at half of the truck's curb weight. That puts the limit for an unbraked trailer at around 700 to 800 pounds for an older Kei truck, including the trailer.

That's as close as you can get without a written capacity from the manufacturer. You will find people online who insist they can tow more with their Kei truck, but just because some random person claims to have regularly towed over 1,000 pounds without wrecking their Kei truck doesn't mean that you should try it with yours. Nor should you go by the rated capacity of an aftermarket tow hitch. That is the rating of the tow hitch, not of your vehicle. Overall, it's best to stick to light towing when it comes to Kei trucks.

On the other hand, the towing capacities of UTVs are typically straightforward. You'll find the capacities listed in their specs, and those specs vary from model to model. For example, the Polaris Ranger XD 1500 NorthStar is rated to tow 3,500 pounds, while the Honda Pioneer 520 is rated to tow 1,000 pounds. If your towing needs involve heavy loads, UTVs are probably the way to go.

You can use either type of vehicle off-road. This is where side-by-sides shine, though, as they were designed specifically for handling rough terrain. Let's start with the tires. You can see from pictures of Kei trucks that they usually come fitted with small street tires that look like they belong on a compact car. UTV tires, on the other hand, often look like tractor tires or tires that go on an ATV. They are made to kick up mud and to laugh at messy terrain.

Clearance is another difference between mini trucks and side-by-sides. The Suzuki Carry mini truck has a ground clearance of around 6 inches. However, the ground clearance for the Honda Pioneer 520 side-by-side is 8.7 inches. The ground clearance for the Polaris Ranger XP 1000 is 14 inches. Of course, the drivetrain is also important when it comes to handling off-road terrain. It's not hard to find a used Kei truck with 4WD. UTVs are typically equipped with AWD, and some can switch between multiple drive modes.

While UTVs excel at off-road performance, we can't say that Kei trucks have to stick to the street. The inclusion of 4WD allows them to hold their own. They are well suited for hard-packed soil, gravel roads, some construction sites, and level ground. But if you have really rough, uneven ground, deep muddy ruts, large rocks, and other obstacles to deal with, our money is on the UTVs.

It probably seems obvious that mini trucks would hold the advantage when it comes to street legality. After all, Kei trucks were made for streets, while side-by-sides were made for off-roading. It's not that simple, though. Sure, the federal government allows Kei trucks that are at least 25 years old to be imported, but that doesn't mean they are road-legal in your state.

Colorado, for example, does not currently allow Kei vehicles to be registered or titled, but that changes on January 1, 2028. After that, Kei vehicles will be allowed on Colorado roads that have a speed limit of 55 miles per hour or less. Pennsylvania allows mini trucks to be registered only with an off-road title, with a farm exemption, or with an antique registration, unless the owner holds a grandfathered registration from 2021. Imported Kei vehicles at least 25 years old are now fully road-legal in Alaska.

Side-by-sides are actually street-legal in certain states. Arizona will issue a motorcycle-style plate to UTVs that have been specifically modified for street use. South Dakota has a similar law. In Colorado, counties and towns decide whether side-by-sides can use their roads, and some towns allow them only during certain hours. Trails are a different matter. The controlling authority for each patch of land that has trails determines which kinds of vehicles are allowed on them. The bottom line is to check the laws of your locality before deciding which vehicle to purchase.

In all of the excitement of finding a mini truck or buying a new side-by-side, it's easy to forget to think about the cost and time that need to go into maintaining these vehicles. Fortunately, maintenance isn't that hard for either type of vehicle. There are some things you want to consider, however.

The recommended frequency of maintenance for side-by-sides is similar to that of motorcycles. Polaris, for example, recommends that the first service for a new Ranger 1000 happen around the 25-hour or 500-mile mark and that the oil and filter then be changed every 200 hours, 2,000 miles, or year, whichever comes first. It's recommended to service the vehicle twice as frequently if it's been exposed to a lot of mud, water, or sand, which is kind of odd, considering that's exactly what side-by-sides are usually exposed to. One of the advantages of UTVs, though, is that you can buy one that is new enough to be under warranty.

The service schedule for Kei trucks is generally not quite as frequent, and their simple engines are easy to work on. But we are talking about a 25-year-old vehicle here. Expect things to go wrong, like worn-out cooling systems, rusted parts of the frame, and vacuum lines that need replacing. Parts are surprisingly easy to find, though you may have to order some of them online. But most of us who work on our own cars have often done that, anyway.

It's hard to compare apples to apples when we talk about the pricing for these vehicles. Any road-legal Kei truck you purchase in the U.S. will be at least 25 years old. It's not likely that you're going to look for a side-by-side that is that old. They are also built for different uses on different terrains.

You can find 25- to nearly 40-year-old Suzuki Carry trucks on Autotrader for anywhere from $7,000 to over $12,000. That's wild, considering you could get a brand-new Carry in Japan for around $7,500 to $10,000. On top of that, you're likely to have to make repairs right off the bat, since the truck is so old. A brand-new Polaris Ranger 1000 UTV costs more, starting around $15,000. But that comes with a 12-month warranty. We found late-model used UTVs on Autotrader and ATV Trader that were priced about the same as much older Kei trucks.

So, which is the better deal? Who's to say? If you're just looking at age and wear and how it lines up with total cost, side-by-sides have a definite advantage. But that doesn't mean they represent the better deal for you personally. Paying a little more for a vehicle that is ideally suited for your uses is a better deal than paying less for a vehicle that doesn't quite fit your needs. Do your research, evaluate how and where you'll use the vehicle, and then make the purchase that's right for you.

#5610. Trump Admin Pauses Enforcement of Its Medicaid Work Rules

— States have gotten a reprieve from the looming January 1 deadline

President Donald Trump's administration told states Friday that they can wait until July before removing people from Medicaid for failing to meet a work requirement.

The requirement is scheduled to take effect nationally on Jan. 1, 2027, and states have been scrambling to put in place the staffing, training, and technology to implement it by then. The administration clarified that while states still have the option to take action at the beginning of the year, they won't have to kick anyone off or deny coverage for failure to meet the requirement until July 1.

Medicaid is the joint state-federal health insurance program for lower-income people. CMS told state Medicaid directors on Friday that they'll still need to determine whether many enrollees and applicants for benefits are meeting new requirements that they are working, in school, or volunteering.

The move announced Friday gives state social service departments more time to make sure complicated changes are ready to run before there are consequences. CMS said that states are making progress but have implementation challenges.

"I think these extra 6 months are going to give states the ability to respond to the change, and there will be fewer people that lose their coverage due to administrative failures" resulting from states' inability to prepare, Kathy Hempstead, senior policy officer for the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, told AP.

Still, she said it's not clear which states will opt to use the additional time.

Kate McEvoy, executive director of the National Association of Medicaid Directors, said state Medicaid leaders "appreciate the additional flexibility that CMS is providing."

The decision also could give some breathing room to Congress to consider changes to the requirement. Democrats who are taking control of both chambers in January after their sweeping election victories last week have said they want to roll back the requirements.

The news comes after Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), and Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. (D-NJ) wrote to CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, MD, MBA, this week, asking to delay implementing the work reporting requirements. Their letter cites, in part, a recent decision out of a Boston federal court that determined medically frail people should not be bound by the work requirement qualification rules.

"The practical reality is that this significant implementation issue may not be definitively resolved for months, creating untenable uncertainty for states that need a final resolution of this issue before going live with work reporting requirements," the letter states. "The court ruling is an important victory for the millions of medically frail people who rely on Medicaid for their healthcare coverage."

Under the policy, many Medicaid beneficiaries must work or volunteer at least 80 hours a month or be in school at least half-time. The new policy applies only to people who receive Medicaid under a voluntary expansion that 40 states undertook and which was intended to get health coverage to more lower-income adults who don't have kids at home. There are exceptions for those who are over age 64, caring for kids under age 14 years, or deemed too medically frail to work.

Critics say that most enrollees covered by the mandate are already working and that people are more likely to lose coverage because of the paperwork to prove it rather than failing to work.

The federal government is pushing states to use data from other government departments or elsewhere to verify whether beneficiaries are working as a way to reduce the burden on the beneficiaries to show proof.

A few states have launched the work requirements early.

The first of them was Nebraska, where they started in May.

Preliminary data presented to the state's Medicaid Advisory Committee showed that more than nine in 10 people subject to the work requirement and due to have their benefits renewed in July and August qualified.

But 533 people were denied continuing coverage. For most of them, it was over paperwork: They didn't show that they were working or were exempt from the requirement. Of those denied, 43 lost coverage because they did not meet the new requirement.

Similarly, most of the new Medicaid applicants who were denied coverage due to work requirements from May through August did not get the coverage because they did not provide information to verify whether they were complying.

Among both groups, it's not clear how many people didn't provide information because they weren't working -- or how many might meet the requirements but failed to show it.

"There are likely people who are still eligible for coverage who lost it," said Amy Behnke, CEO of the Health Care Center Association of Nebraska.

He writes Neurotransmissions, a STAT column about the new era of dementia.

This is the second of two pieces about the experiencing of pre-clinical Alzheimer’s. Read the first here.

In 1976, at the dawn of the modern Alzheimer’s era, the neurologist Robert Katzman, champion of efforts to extract Alzheimer’s from senility and “normal aging,” concluded his short essay “The prevalence and malignancy of Alzheimer disease” with this notably qualified call to action:

“In focusing attention on the mortality associated with Alzheimer disease, our goal is not to find a way to prolong the life of severely demented persons, but rather to call attention to our belief that senile as well as presenile forms of Alzheimer are a single disease, a disease whose etiology must be determined, whose course must be aborted, and ultimately a disease to be prevented.”

#5608. Weekly Rundown: Ohio State Wexner, Microsoft ink tech deal; OpenEvidence launches free Access Intelligence tools

Weekly Rundown: Ohio State Wexner, Microsoft ink tech deal; OpenEvidence launches free Access Intelligence tools" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stay up to date on the latest in health tech, digital health and health AI news with this weekly brief. Read below for news from the week of Nov. 9 to 13.

Revenue management company R1 expanded Thursday its revenue operating system Phare OS with six connected AI solutions to bring agentic automation across pre- and post-bill healthcare operations

Four of the tools are now commercially available: Phare Auth, Phare Audit, Phare UM and a new Phare Denials module. Meanwhile, executives say Phare CDI and Phare Recovery are in early access with select customers—with broader availability expected in 2027.

“We’ve established Phare OS as the foundation for a different model of revenue management where technology isn’t measured by how many tasks it automates, but by the results it delivers,” said Joe Flanagan, R1 CEO, in a statement. “After decades of helping providers navigate the complexity of [the] revenue cycle, we know what it takes to improve performance. We’re bringing that expertise together with AI and payer intelligence, and we stand behind the outcomes. This is the level of accountability health systems should expect from their revenue management partners.”

OpenEvidence announced Wednesday the launch of Access Intelligence, a slate of tools built directly into its platform that allows clinicians to access affordability and coverage information.

Access Intelligence is free to all clinicians and can answer questions about availability and eligibility on more than 2,500 patient support programs, like copay savings and patient assistance, the company says. Other key features include:

The company says the suite will “continue to evolve to best support clinicians through the complex affordability and coverage landscape.”

“Programs exist to help patients with treatment access, and prior authorizations can be won, but the process is so fragmented and time-consuming that engaging with it is nearly impossible,” said Ania Bilski, M.D., OpenEvidence clinical AI vice president, in a statement. “Access Intelligence is our commitment to helping physicians and patients close the loop of care, from identifying support programs to completing enrollment to getting a prior authorization approved. Choosing the right treatment should be the hard part. Getting the patient access to it shouldn’t be.”

The Ohio State University and Microsoft announced Tuesday a five-year strategic partnership that aims to accelerate innovation across clinical care settings, education and research.

“Artificial intelligence represents one of the most significant opportunities to transform and improve how hospitals care for patients,” said John Warner, M.D., Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center CEO, in a statement. “Through this collaboration, we have an opportunity to help reimagine the future of healthcare as we bring together Ohio State’s academic medical expertise with Microsoft’s technological capabilities to accelerate the pace of innovation across patient care, research and education.”

Microsoft and the Ohio State Wexner Medical Center are co-developing a smart hospital model through the partnership, while also modernizing clinical and research applications and workloads through the cloud, unifying data and using AI to support care teams.

The American Medical Association (AMA) adopted a policy on Monday that declares AI can be used to aid physicians and assist with clinical tasks, but cannot be granted licensure, professional titles or certifications to practice medicine.

Moreover, the organization said it will advocate for legislation that establishes a framework for physician oversight of AI clinical-decision making. The organization also is calling for protections for physicians when AI tools cause patient harm.

AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., said in a statement that "patients deserve to know who is responsible for their care."

"Physicians also need the authority, oversight and liability protections to make independent decisions when AI is part of the care team," Underwood said.

Identity verification company Clear launched Monday two integrations within the Epic Toolbox, which will allow health systems to verify outside providers and prescribing clinicians.

The company’s CLEAR1 identity platform is now available through Epic Toolbox for EpicCare Link and electronic prescribing of controlled substances. The prescribing integration is available in Epic’s End User Authentication category.

“Doctors and nurses shouldn't spend their shifts proving who they are,” said David Bardan, CLEAR SVP, general manager and head of healthcare, in a statement. “Getting into a patient's chart and prescribing a controlled medication are two more places they no longer have to start from scratch. We're using secure identity to make healthcare safer and easier for care teams, from the first day to the first patient, and every shift after.”

Ellipsis Health, a voice AI care management company, acquired Kouper Health, a startup that built AI agents deeply embedded in clinical workflows.

Kouper's AI agents work inside health system electronic health record (EHR) systems like Athenahealth and Epic to coordinate care from scheduling through discharge and follow-up.

The deal pairs Ellipsis's "emotionally intelligent" AI voice care manager, Sage, with Kouper's native EHR integrations and longitudinal patient maps to deliver continuous, connected patient care, according to the companies.

Ellipsis Health works with seven of the top 20 health plans in the U.S. and leading academic medical centers and integrated delivery networks.

Founded in 2022, Kouper has raised funding from investors including CVS Health Ventures, General Catalyst and 25madison. Its technology embeds AI agents into health system workflows and builds longitudinal patient maps that bring information from across a patient’s care into a more unified view. Ellipsis' Sage can pick up from there with discharge follow-ups, medication adherence support and clinical check-ins by phone and text. Sage is used by nine of the top 15 U.S. health plans and has delivered up to 7x ROI for customers, the company said.

Sage is powered by a patented "empathy engine" trained on over 3 million labeled clinical conversations. It analyzes vocal cues in real time to assess emotional signals and adapt its interactions. Through phone and text, Sage supports care management tasks including enrollment, clinical assessments, medication adherence and post-discharge follow-up.

Kouper’s team is joining Ellipsis. Both companies will continue serving existing customers under their respective brands while developing a combined product roadmap, with new offerings for health systems expected in the months ahead.

“Healthcare has enormous potential to benefit from AI, but the hard part has been making that technology work for patients and care teams,” said Mainul Mondal, founder and CEO of Ellipsis Health, in a statement. “We have extraordinary clinicians, but we can’t solve access and continuity problems by asking them to do more. Kouper brings critical infrastructure for making that possible inside health systems. By combining their native integrations and longitudinal patient maps with Sage’s emotional intelligence, we can help care teams extend their reach and deliver more continuous, personalized support.”

#5607. Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer; AI-Enabled Prior Auth; Type 1 Diabetes Subtypes

TTHealthWatch is a weekly podcast from Texas Tech. In it, Elizabeth Tracey, director of electronic media for Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore, and Rick Lange, MD, president of Texas Tech Health El Paso, look at the top medical stories of the week.

This week's topics include early-onset colorectal cancer, artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled prior authorization, T cells and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and different metabolic subtypes of adult type 1 diabetes.

0:41 Subtypes of type 1 diabetes in adults

6:16 Increased stromal-to-epithelial ratio

7:50 Was a change in frequency of procedure

10:10 Cerebrospinal (CSF) versus circulation

11:20 Cytomegalovirus interacts with existing conditions

Elizabeth: What are the differences between early-onset colorectal cancer and that that occurs in older people?

Rick: Does AI-enabled prior authorization change clinical practice?

Elizabeth: What's the role of T cells in ALS?

Rick: And different metabolic subtypes of adult type 1 diabetes.

Elizabeth: That's what we're talking about this week on TTHealthWatch, your weekly look at the medical headlines from Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center in El Paso. I'm Elizabeth Tracey, a Baltimore-based medical journalist.

Rick: And I'm Rick Lange, president of Texas Tech Health El Paso.

Elizabeth: Rick, why don't we turn to The Lancet? I find this notion of, gosh, subtypes of type 1 diabetes to be pretty intriguing.

Rick: Most often when we talk about type 1 diabetes, we talk about it in kids, and it's an autoimmune disease. There are antibodies that form against the beta cells that cause their death and decrease insulin, and therefore result in diabetes. But the same thing can happen in adults. It looks like there's a lot of different heterogeneity, different clinical presentations. Are these distinct disease entities, or are they just different stages of a shared autoimmune process?

They did a prospective cohort study. They analyzed data from adults aged 18 to 69 that were in the German Diabetes Study that had clinically diagnosed type 1 within the preceding 12 months. And then they asked whether the results were reproducible in a prospective follow-up of the same patients. They assessed different antibodies, their triglycerides, their HDL, and tried to characterize clinical and metabolic subtypes. And then they looked at insulin sensitivity, residual B-cell function, and looked at the trajectory.

And what they discovered is that there were three distinct subtypes. Two had antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase -- I'm going to call it GADA -- and one was GADA-negative. I want to focus on the GADA-positive. They characterized these into two different groups. One was what they called classic type 1 diabetes. These were adults that had a lower BMI [body mass index], high insulin sensitivity, and severe B-cell dysfunction. And the second group that were GADA-positive, they had a higher BMI, lower insulin sensitivity, and they had better B-cell function. They call those the mixed type 1 diabetes.

It appeared that the mixed type 1 diabetes was actually just an earlier form of the classic, about 6 years earlier. If we can identify these individuals, and if we know it's an immune response, perhaps doing immunomodulatory therapy can change things.

Elizabeth: A couple questions about this. I'm always wondering about, gosh, why didn't anyone ever look at this before to see about this heterogeneity, which certainly we see every time we look at something that presents clinically in a certain way. Gosh, there's an awful lot under there; that's that iceberg notion. The other thing is you didn't mention the negative, the other group.

Rick: Yep. It takes a large number of patients, a large amount of data, and you have to do a cluster analysis. And if we take these similarities, then what are the differences between this similar group and that similar group?

Not only are there differences with regard to GADA and the timing of when the diabetes is likely to occur, there was also differences with the risk of hypoglycemia, retinopathy, and cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy. And in fact, they were higher in the mixed group than they were in the classic group.

With regard to the GADA-negative group, had other different antibodies that were responsible for their diabetes. The B-cell function was intermediate between the other two groups. There was a more gradual beta-cell decline, a lower diabetes genetic risk, and reduced islet cell autoimmunity, suggesting it was pathogenetically different and also heterogeneous.

Elizabeth: Clearly, this has important clinical implications and needs to be distilled into something that can be just tested pretty routinely and then employed.

Rick: Yep. When you identify an adult with type 1 diabetes, if we can catch them very early in that disease, when they're in the mixed-diabetes group, we can change their immune system and either delay or prevent progression of the disease.

Elizabeth: Let's turn from here then, speaking of things that happen early in life, to Nature Medicine. And this is a study looking at insights into early-onset colorectal cancer from a single-nucleus RNA-sequencing atlas of colorectal cancer across the age continuum.

What these folks did was they looked at 189 primary colorectal cancer tumors spanning eight decades of life with at least 20 tumors in most age decades. They did a number of analyses on this, stratifying tumors by their microsatellite status, the tumor sidedness in the person, the stage, the patient's sex, neoadjuvant treatment history.

What they found was that tumors from the younger patients were characterized by increased stromal and decreased epithelial proportions. They confirmed that in an external cohort of 712 colorectal cancer tumors. Epithelial cells from the younger patients demonstrated increased expression of what are called long non-coding RNAs, a trend toward increased heterogeneity and copy number alterations. Left-sided colorectal cancer tumors had more cell-to-cell interactions.

What they basically conclude is yes, indeed, there are things that we can look at. This stromal versus epithelial proportion and the sidedness seem to be distinguishing characteristics, and maybe help further understand why this is happening more often in younger people.

Rick: The incidence of colorectal cancer before the age of 50 has been increasing about 1 to 3% per year. It is now the leading cause of cancer death in adults 18 to 49 years of age. Unfortunately, the survival of individuals with early colorectal cancer is poor. Part of it's poor because 58% of these individuals are in late stages of the disease, but also, as you mentioned, we're trying to distinguish are there characteristics from the tumor that make it more resistant to therapy?

This increased stromal-to-epithelial ratio -- there's more connective tissue and less cells -- makes it more resistant to standard chemotherapy. So identifying these individuals early and identifying unique markers that may be more responsive to particular types of therapy are important.

Elizabeth: Clearly points to the need to develop new treatments that are targeted toward these particular characteristics versus the ones that have been classically identified.

Rick: Are these targets of treatment, and are they actually driving the tumor, or are they just bystanders?

Rick: AI-enabled prior authorization and particularly in Medicare.

This is really controversial because prior authorization requires the clinician to submit a justification for a specific medical service. The reason it's controversial is commercial insurers use this as a way of denying insurance and denying payment. If the procedure is necessary, that's really frustrating to the patient and to the physician, obviously. And in the past, Medicare has not required any prior authorizations with rare exceptions.

However, in January of this year, CMS initiated what's called the Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction, called the WISeR model, talking about prior authorization, to make sure that the procedure that's being done is not wasteful and it's not inappropriate because these are services that are considered vulnerable to fraud, waste, and abuse.

So what Medicare said is, OK, we're going to use AI-enabled prior authorization for some particular procedures, one being epidural steroid injection. Before we're going to reimburse hospitals or physicians for this particular procedure, we're going to submit these individuals to prior authorization using AI to do that. Did that really change the use of epidural steroid injection? And by the way, we're going to compare the six states in whom AI authorization was enacted with all the other states.

When they looked at it, the use of AI authorization led to a 15% reduction relative to the baseline use of epidural steroid injection. Did the other procedures that didn't require authorization change? Not at all. Just the ones in whom prior authorization was used. It looked like there was a dip and then there was a recovery. The question is, over the next 6 months, will that maintain or not? Is it just because there's a new process and it slowed things down, and now it's going to recur? Or does it actually do what it's supposed to do? Make sure the test is both appropriate and not wasteful.

Elizabeth: As we know, AI models train. And so one question I have is, as this thing trains and it gathers more data, and perhaps there are more people who push back and say, oh, wait a second, this is really indicated here, there might be a training impact as well.

Rick: Yeah. You're right. So this is a 6-year project. So we're going to want to follow it for a long period of time. This is just the initial results from the first two quarters, more data to come.

Elizabeth: OK. Turning back to Nature Medicine then, let's take a look at this notion of T cell involvement in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS.

This study is looking at T-cell responses in folks who have it. Previous research has implicated T cells here. And what they're using is single-cell RNA and T-cell receptor sequencing, longitudinal immune profiling, and imaging flow cytometry to identify long-lived intrathecal clonotypes and antigen-presenting T-cell complexes that have features of immunological synapse formation.

What they find is that, sure enough, in the CSF, in the cerebrospinal fluid, they do find these higher frequencies of different subtypes of T cells there that were associated with slower disease progression. Whereas when they noted that these same subtypes of CD4 cells, the T cells, were found in the circulation, they were associated with faster progression of ALS.

They did find that there were also these differences in T-cell clonotypes that were shared between the blood and the CSF exhibited distinct transcriptional states. They also noted that cytomegalovirus-specific T cells in the cerebrospinal fluid and serum antibodies were associated with faster progression and shorter survival in the sporadic form of ALS, which is the majority of the cases, I would note, versus that that's genetically associated. I, at least, am happy to see further characterization of this disease and potentially ways that might point to an intervention.

Rick: Yeah. Neuroinflammation is now recognized as being an important part of the central feature of ALS. About three-fourths of the cases are sporadic, about a fourth are from mutations, and ALS from a complex interplay between both genetic susceptibility and environmental influences that causes neuroinflammation. And, by the way, cytomegalovirus probably isn't the thing that initiates it, it just interacts with all this together. The fact that we can identify different types of T cells, those that regulate or those that help promote inflammation, those different populations in the blood and in the brain hopefully will give us some insight in how best to modulate the neuroinflammation.

Elizabeth: Or even to slow it down. I was gratified to see that the authors of this study did look at other neurotropic viruses and assess their role. So they looked specifically at herpes viruses and they found that this was specific to cytomegalovirus.

One of the questions I have, of course, is that cytomegalovirus is just so very common. What is that interaction? And if it was really a pronounced interaction, I would think that ALS would be a good deal more common than it is.

Rick: Yeah. It's not a uniform driver of pathology, but it interacts with the underlying disease mechanisms. It's a very complicated interplay in terms of the neuroinflammatory response.

On that note then, that's a look at this week's medical headlines from Texas Tech. I'm Elizabeth Tracey.

Rick: And I'm Rick Lange. Y'all listen up and make healthy choices.

#5606. Dyania Health, Nvidia team up to bring clinical reasoning AI inside hospital networks

Dyania Health, Nvidia team up to bring clinical reasoning AI inside hospital networks" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Dyania Health is partnering with Nvidia to run its Synapsis AI clinical reasoning platform inside hospitals’ IT systems, enabling large-scale analysis without patient data leaving their networks.

The startup's Synapsis AI reads a patient's full medical record, including clinical notes, imaging and operative reports, labs and other largely unstructured information, and answers clinical questions while pointing back to supporting evidence in the chart. Dyania Health goes beyond summarizing medical records; it uses AI to convert messy, unstructured clinical records into usable datasets and insights.

Nvidia provides the computing infrastructure needed to perform that analysis across potentially entire patient populations behind the hospital firewall, without transferring patient records outside the health system, according to the company.

Dyania brings the clinical reasoning technology and implementation expertise, while Nvidia brings the accelerated computing platform and the software that lets it run securely and efficiently on-premises, Eirini Schlosser, founder and CEO of Dyania Health, told Fierce Healthcare.

Through this collaboration with Nvidia, Dyania's Synapsis AI could help health systems turn large volumes of unstructured clinical data into actionable insights at a scale that would be impractical with manual chart review, while keeping patient data inside the hospital’s own infrastructure, Schlosser said.

Health systems have vast amounts of valuable clinical information locked in unstructured medical records, but manually reviewing those records makes it difficult to use that data at scale for research, registries and predictive models. Synapsis AI aims to remove that bottleneck by analyzing patients’ records longitudinally, determining what happened and when, and identifying the clinical evidence supporting those conclusions, according to the company, which launched out of stealth two years ago.

Frontier models are becoming extraordinarily capable, but the architectures, training data sets, as well as logic are not built to perform clinical reasoning in a real-world healthcare system environment, Schlosser noted.

Dyania's Synapsis AI combines specialized models, a clinician-annotated clinical knowledge base, evidence tracing and hospital-specific implementation. Dyania says it has invested more than 25,000 physician hours annotating medical cases so that Synapsis AI can perform clinical reasoning. This specialized approach is better suited to complex clinical reasoning than a single general-purpose AI model, Schlosser asserted.

"Every patient's story is spread across years of notes, reports and results, and for the first time we can reason across all of it at once, the way a specialist does, for every patient in a health system rather than one chart at a time,” Schlosser said.

Synapsis AI is built on the Nvidia AI enterprise software stack end to end. Dyania trains its proprietary clinical models with the Nvidia NeMo framework for model training and reinforcement learning. Inside the health system, Synapsis AI runs on Nvidia TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM on the hospital's own accelerated computing infrastructure, so inference stays inside the hospital's private network.

Hospitals can use their own historical patient data to determine which treatments work for which patients, identify care gaps and ultimately recommend the next appropriate action, according to Schlosser.

Under the collaboration, the companies will work to bring Synapsis AI on Nvidia infrastructure to health systems in the U.S. and internationally, publish joint case studies and integrate Synapsis AI with Nvidia's healthcare software stack. The companies are exploring additional Nvidia technologies to secure AI processing, handle multiple clinical workloads at once and scale computing capacity, with the goal of moving from batch processing toward near-real-time clinical insights at the point of care.

"Health systems need AI they can trust, integrate into their workflows and operate efficiently. That means connecting information across clinical systems, validating performance for the patients they serve, protecting sensitive data and making results useful within the tools clinicians already use," Chelsea Sumner, Nvidia's U.S. healthcare AI startups ecosystem lead, told Fierce Healthcare.

"Dyania’s approach addresses part of that challenge by running inside the hospital’s own environment and linking findings to evidence in the patient record. Scaling also requires clinicians, technology teams and hospital leaders to work together from the start, with clear responsibility for reviewing results and monitoring performance. Success should be measured by whether AI helps teams find patients who need attention, make better-informed decisions and spend more time delivering care," Sumner said.

Cleveland Clinic used Dyania Health’s Synapsis AI, running on Nvidia infrastructure, to analyze up to 16 years of records from 7,812 aortic valve replacement patients. The study addressed a central concern for patients: How long will the replacement valve last, and will another procedure be needed?

Researchers reviewed nearly 8,000 patient records between 2005 and 2021, mostly narrative notes and echocardiogram reports that registries can struggle to capture.

"Understanding how a replacement heart valve performs means following a patient across years of care, connecting the original operative report with subsequent progress notes, hospitalizations, echocardiograms, other medical conditions and later interventions. Much of that information is buried in narrative records that researchers would otherwise need to review manually," Schlosser noted.

The AI extracted information from narrative clinical records and answered 88 questions per patient about their valves, health conditions and subsequent care. Each answer linked to supporting evidence in the chart, he noted.

Researchers used that dataset to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and the risk of another intervention. The model estimates valve deterioration and repeat-procedure risk at three, five and 10 years post-procedure, with estimates that update as new medical information about the patient becomes available.

"Historically, this would have required human manual abstraction, and for 7,812 patients, it would be humanly impossible to read and abstract features on an ongoing basis at the rate at which medical records are changing. Additionally, humans reading a medical record can often miss information if they skim through it," Schlosser said.

The tool is used to help inform care but requires external validation from clinicians.

"Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients," said Lars G. Svensson, M.D., Ph.D., chief of the Heart, Vascular and Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic, in a statement.

The health system began working with Dyania Health a year ago to use its AI platform for clinical trial recruitment.

Synapsis AI made it possible for the first time to comprehensively analyze nearly two decades of patient data, Schlosser asserted. "What was even more groundbreaking was the ability to go from raw data in unstructured form to predictive risk models in one fell swoop. This enables precision care at scale and empowers physicians with stronger sets of information backing their clinical decisions about any given patient, including questions like 'when should the patient have their next echo?' or 'when will the patient likely need a reintervention?'" Schlosser said.

The Cleveland Clinic and Dyania Health collaboration reflects Nvidia's broader focus to provide healthcare and life sciences innovators with the computing platform and AI tools to advance research and help care teams better understand patients’ needs, Sumner said.

The heart valve study shows how Synapsis AI could help health systems use their own patient data to determine which treatments work best for which patients and improve predictive models over time, ultimately supporting more personalized care recommendations, according to Dyania Health.

"Nvidia's infrastructure enables us to handle more work concurrently and use resources more efficiently. That could allow hospitals to examine larger populations, ask more detailed questions and revisit analyses more frequently. The longer-term opportunity is to move from periodic batches of records toward insights available closer to the moment a clinician needs them," Schlosser said.

"We can do that within the health system’s own environment, keeping patient records behind its firewall. We are also evaluating capabilities for distributed inference, workload isolation and protection of data during computation. Computing power alone does not make a clinical conclusion correct; it allows a carefully developed clinical system to work at greater scale and speed," he said.

Sumner asserts that healthcare organizations are just scratching the surface on the potential for AI to uncover clinically useful information buried in longitudinal patient records.

"Connecting a physician’s notes with earlier test results and treatment history could help identify patients who need follow-up, match people with clinical trials and give researchers a clearer understanding of how treatments perform over time," she said. "The Cleveland Clinic heart valve study is a concrete example. AI helped researchers assemble a detailed view of patients’ care to study how replacement valves deteriorate. The opportunity is to turn that knowledge into more personalized monitoring and better-informed care decisions. Clinicians need to be able to review the supporting evidence, validate the findings and decide what they mean for each patient."

#5605. Rocket Fuel: The Last Frontier For Natural Gas

Fossil fuels are slowly beginning to lose their grip on the global transportation sector, with one key omission: rocket fuel. The rocket fuel conundrum has earned an uptick in attention in recent years, now that rocket launches, once rare, are becoming as commonplace as rush hour traffic. The Elon Musk venture SpaceX, for example, is building new natural gas pipelines in order to produce its own methane-based propellant, needed to sustain the launch of many thousands of rockets in the coming years.

Not all rocket fuel is methane-based, but that’s where some aerospace firms, including SpaceX, have landed in the pursuit of space domination. Methane is processed from natural gas, stripping away nitrogen and other impurities. Liquefied and mixed with liquid oxygen, it becomes a powerful propellant.

With its future volume of launch operations in mind, SpaceX aims to exercise as much control as possible over its fuel supply. The company is investing in its own natural gas pipelines and on-site fuel production facilities to help ensure that the taps don’t run dry, though it still relies on the gas industry to find the stuff and bring it up from the ground.

SpaceX has already been sucking up a copious amount of natural gas for its existing operations in Texas and Florida. “SpaceX (SPCX) is emerging as one of the largest new customers for natural gas,” reported the oil and gas analytics firm East Daley in October.

“Unlike Falcon 9, which burns rocket-grade kerosene and liquid oxygen, Starship creates a direct link between launch activity and natural gas consumption. SPCX plans to process and liquefy pipeline gas into liquid methane to fuel the rockets,” East Daley elaborates.

As described by East Daley, the SpaceX subsidiary Coastal Connect Services is planning a 32.4-mile natural gas pipeline to hook up SpaceX operations in Cape Canaveral, Florida with existing infrastructure jointly owned by Kinder Morgan and Energy Transfer.

Meanwhile, at the company’s launch site and newly incorporated (as of 2025) City of Starbase in Cameron County, Texas, plans are in motion for SpaceX affiliate Lone Star Mineral Development to connect the new 8-mile “Starpipe” natural gas pipeline with another 145-mile pipeline currently being built by the firms WhiteWater, Enbridge, and MPLX. Starpipe is expected to begin shuttling natural gas into Starbase Texas early next year.

The two pipeline projects come alongside word that SpaceX has nailed down approvals for parts of a new $100 billion project that expands the company’s US footprint into another combination city-and-launch-site under the name of Starbase, Louisiana. The new city will presumably also require a reliable supply of natural gas for on-site rocket fuel production.

For the record, Starbase, Louisiana is not part of the educational non-profit organization STARBASE Louisiana, an affiliate of the national STARBASE program of the US Department of Defense, aimed at stimulating interest in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics) topics among 5th grade students. The Louisiana branch of STARBASE is located Barksdale Air Force Base in Bossier Parish, in the northwestern part of the state.

Starbase, Louisiana will take up 125,000 acres of land at Pecan Island in a marshy region along the southern coast in Vermilion Parish, where plans are being laid for 30 launches per day. More than a dozen launch towers will eventually sprout up at the site, where the operation will include producing rocket fuel.

If you’ve gotten wind of the project under the name “Osprey,” you’re not dreaming. The new city was reportedly code-named “Project Osprey” during initial discussions with public officials. As described by the Gulf State News affiliate WWNO (New Orleans Public Radio) on November 11, Project Osprey was shrouded in secrecy during the initial negotionas, with “dozens” of local officials signing non-disclosure agreements that limited what they could say about the project.

The Osprey code name also reportedly enabled Vermilion Parish officials to sidestep public participation in ostensibly public hearings on the Starbase, Louisiana project earlier this year. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry finally let the cat out of the bag in a public announcement in August. Local residents and the nonprofit organization Vermillion Citizens coalition have already filed a lawsuit against the project, alleging that parish officials approved parts of Starbase, Louisiana in violation of the state’s Open Public Meetings Law.

If and when shovels hit the ground on Starbase, Louisiana, the Trump administration is taking steps to help ensure that natural gas producers in the US come through with the goods — not just for SpaceX, of course, although the firm has become a market-mover in the gas industry as noted by East Daley.

On November 10, for example, the US Department of Energy announced the finishing touches on a $480 million loan in support of Project Elkhorn, an endeavor under the umbrella of the oil and gas firm Arena Energy. Project Elkhorn covers the modernization of 22 existing platforms off the Louisiana coast — coincidentally or not, the same state that expects to host the new Starbase city.

Arena launched in 1999 with a focus on revitalizing mature oil and gas fields. According to the Energy Department, Project Elkhorn will ramp natural gas production up to 77 million cubic feet per day at peak production among the 22 platforms, alongside up to 38,600 barrels of oil per day. By way of contrast, the 22 platforms currently produce 30,000 barrels of oil per day. Over the lifespan of Project Elkhorn, the collective total is expected to add 25 million barrels of oil and 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas to the US fossil energy roster.

As CEO of the leading EV maker Tesla, Elon Musk has earned his share of credit for rescuing electric cars from the dustbin of automotive obscurity and vaulting them into the mainstream mobility market of today — if not so much here in the US, then certainly overseas. Musk’s other ventures, on the other hand, threaten to offset, if not override, whatever sustainability gains are to be made from EVs.

In addition to SpaceX, Musk’s xAI data centers have also contributed to spiking demand for natural gas. Last year word dropped that Musk’s Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee trucked in approximately three dozen industrial-sized gas generators to power the site, at least 15 of which were already in operation without an air quality permit. The Southern Environmental Law Center has been among those raising the alarm over toxic emissions from the generators, which lack the pollution controls required of permanent power plants.

Natural gas also factors into a new data center planned for the SpaceX-backed City of Starbase, Texas, which sits adjacent to Brownsville. The city of Brownsville recently imposed a temporary moratorium on new data center construction. According to ABC News affiliate KVUE and other sources, earlier this year Elon Musk asked Brownsville officials to de-annex a parcel of land at its outskirts, evidently in order to building a $24 billion data center at the site along with a new gas-fired power plant for a new data center to be located in Starbase. The request was granted, enabling the project to skirt around the Brownsville moratorium.

Starbase city officials are scheduled to conduct a public hearing on the new data center on December 9, where presumably they will decide whether or not the project can make due with gas generators until a full gas power plant with appropriate pollution controls can materialize.

Over and above the rocket fuel issue, grassroots activists, environmental organizations, and researchers have been raising the alarm over the impact of Starbase in Texas for years, tracking significant harm to local public recreation resources as well as wildlife habitats. Similar concerns have surfaced around SpaceX’s plans for Starbase, Louisiana.

Of course, nobody seriously expects the whole domestic rocket business to stop in its tracks. The issue is one of mitigating climate and biodiversity risks, developing projects that avoid pummeling vulnerable communities with additional public health risks, and investing in more sustainable options including alternative rocket fuels.

Keep an eye on the aviation industry for some hints at the future of sustainable propellants. Airline stakeholders have been focusing on SAF, generally meaning a bio-based equivalent of kerosene jet fuel. However, the going has been slow, and it’s even slower in the field of propellants. The European Space Agency, for example, has been exploring green propellants for space operations for 25 years, with little to show for its efforts.

More recently, though, aviation stakeholders have begun turning to the emerging electrofuels or “solar fuels” industry, meaning fuels synthesized from captured carbon and green hydrogen, with solar and other renewables powering the operation. The green hydrogen industry has been struggling for traction, but signs of scaleup have finally emerged, with e-kerosene jet fuel in play along with green hydrogen. Honda, for one, is envisioning a fleet of reusable rockets propelled by renewable fuels, and at least two Chinese firms are also working the reusable rocket angle.

Image: SpaceX is among the industrial-scale consumers of natural gas adding more pipes to the nation’s sprawling network of gas pipelines, which the startup needs to ensure a steady supply of fuel for its growing fleet of rockets (courtesy of US Energy Information Agency).

Tina has been covering advanced energy technology, military sustainability, emerging materials, biofuels, ESG and related policy and political matters for CleanTechnica since 2009. Follow her @tinamcasey on LinkedIn, Mastodon or Bluesky.

#5604. 5 takeaways from STAT’s investigation of the sprawling ‘three-parent IVF’ industry

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Megan covers the intersection of science and society. How is biomedical research funded? Who benefits? And how do new technologies reflect and shape our values? You can reach Megan on Signal at mmolteni.13.

The investigation started with a tip from a British couple.

After trying to have a second child for several years, they had signed up with a U.S.-based company called International Fertility Group (IFG), paying tens of thousands of dollars for access abroad to an experimental fertility procedure illegal in the U.S. and tightly regulated in the U.K. The procedure, known as MRT — for mitochondrial replacement techniques — is sometimes called “three-parent IVF,” because it involves creating embryos that combine the genes of a mother and father with a bit of DNA from the mitochondria of a third person.

In the U.K., MRT is allowed at only one academic medical center, and only for the purposes of lowering the risk of passing on mitochondrial disease. But according to IFG, the procedure could also help older women overcome issues that make the odds of IVF go down significantly after the age of 40. Despite being a doctor herself, the woman in the couple had been taken in by the hope of a miracle.

Her husband reached out to me concerned the claims were unfounded, and hoping STAT could look into it.

Over the past eight months, my reporting took me inside an emerging international MRT tourism industry. It led me to IFG’s headquarters in an office park outside of Chicago and to one of its partners in Albania, an upscale fertility clinic where a Turkish embryologist living in Slovakia would fly in monthly to perform the procedure on IFG clients’ eggs or embryos. With the help of an Albanian journalist, Inva Hasanaliaj, we dug into corporate registration and medical licensing records. Freelance science reporter Edward Chen helped us to gather the stories of current and former IFG clients and interview scientists, including the world’s top MRT researchers.

All of this reporting was undertaken in an effort to understand what is driving demand for this unproven procedure, what risks women are taking to seek it out, and how commercial claims stack up against the science. Here’s what we found.

Currently, there are no peer-reviewed studies in humans supporting the idea that MRT can overcome infertility issues caused by aging, especially in women 35 years and older. A pilot study from a fertility clinic in Greece, published in 2023, reported that MRT could improve live birth rates for women under the age of 40, but the biggest improvements occurred among the youngest patients. For the 12 patients who were 39 at the time of MRT, the live birth rate was less than 10%.

Researchers affiliated with IFG did present some data in a conference abstract for a 2025 European scientific meeting, claiming that among 66 patients with a mean age of 39, live birth rates following MRT reached rates of 40% or higher. But scientists told STAT the abstract lacked key information required to support that claim, and a conference organizer questioned whether it should have been accepted.

The most compelling evidence it might work in older women comes from a single lab study in mice. But even the underlying hypothesis that mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to age-related infertility is supported by very little direct evidence, experts told STAT.

Before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Kyiv was poised to become the MRT capital of the world. Women traveled from Europe, Israel, and the U.S. to at least three clinics there offering it as an infertility treatment. Unpublished data from the Nadiya Clinic — the most advanced operation in Kyiv — shows that a form of MRT called pronuclear transfer did not improve the odds of IVF for older women. Among 19 patients aged 36 to 44, only one gave birth to a baby following pronuclear transfer.

In contrast, among 10 infertile patients under the age of 35, MRT resulted in nine live births.

For the past few years, International Fertility Group has advertised its MRT program as “a groundbreaking fertility treatment that offers renewed hope to women with advanced maternal age or a history of failed cycles.” The company’s social media posts about MRT frequently targeted women over the age of 35, and its own internal data showed its clients were skewing older. According to an IFG webinar from February, the average age of a patient in the company’s MRT program was 39.2 years old in 2022; last year it was 45.6 years old.

After STAT contacted IFG about these materials, which several experts described as “misleading” and “unethical,” the company removed them. In a statement, IFG acknowledged that the evidence for MRT remains limited and emphasized that its role is to provide nonmedical support to patients. “IFG does not characterize innovative treatment as guaranteed, routine, or risk-free,” the statement said. “Patients are not promised a pregnancy, a live birth, or any particular outcome.”

The company’s MRT program is currently on pause. Last week, hours after STAT’s investigation was published, Birol Aydin, the Turkish embryologist who performed the procedure for IFG clients in Albania, announced on LinkedIn that he was stepping back from clinical work to focus on research.

Clinics unaffiliated with IFG operating in Mexico and the Bahamas are continuing to market MRT as a fertility treatment to women 40 and older as a way to combat age-related declines in egg quality. Neither has published any outcome data.

The concerns are twofold. First, that companies are profiting from selling false hope to people with a strong desire to try everything possible to have genetically related children. And second, that children born through commercial MRT won’t be monitored for any adverse health effects that might emerge later in their lives.

Data from the Nadiya Clinic underscore similar results from that 2023 pilot study in Greece, showing that a different form of MRT, called maternal spindle transfer, could help women under the age of 35 with a history of severe infertility get pregnant and have children.

Researchers at Ghent University are currently launching a small study of MRT for addressing these types of fertility failures, which collectively are called OZEMA (for oocyte, zygote, and embryo maturation arrest). Initial results are expected sometime next year. Positive outcomes would add to the increasing pressure to ease restrictions on human trials of MRT for infertility in countries where such studies are currently banned, including the U.S., so that people don’t have to go abroad.

Megan covers the intersection of science and society. How is biomedical research funded? Who benefits? And how do new technologies reflect and shape our values? You can reach Megan on Signal at mmolteni.13.

#5603. 5 Generations Of The Chevy Impala SS Ranked From Best To Worst Horsepower Ratings

Mention a Chevy Impala, and thoughts of an unremarkable family sedan may come to mind, but add an SS next to the nameplate and things change. The Impala SS (Super Sport) is a pure horsepower play that dates back to 1961, two years after the Bowtie brand launched the Impala as a standalone model. Its numbers are still impressive, even by 21st-century standards. The retail version of the Impala SS from the 1960s, which covered two generations, produced up to 425 horsepower. The later Impala SS generations from the 1990s and 2000s were less brutish, offering between 240 and 303 hp, but they were still a step up from their more mundane counterparts.

However, these horsepower numbers come with a catch. The output figures for 1960s Impala SS models reflected gross horsepower ratings, which generally didn't account for intake, exhaust, and accessory loads. When the 1970s rolled around, the auto industry was dealing with tighter emissions regulations and insurance companies that took a dim view of high-powered cars. By the 1972 model year, Detroit switched to net horsepower calculations to better reflect real-world engine configurations. Because gross horsepower ratings often varied from manufacturer to manufacturer, there's no standard way to convert horsepower ratings between the methods, but both still measure horsepower at the crankshaft, not the wheels.

Our ranking of every Impala SS generation by power takes into account the highest advertised horsepower ratings for regular-production SS models, regardless of whether it's gross or net. Special race versions and modified cars are excluded. Here's how every Impala SS generation compares in maximum power output.

The first Impala was a variant of the 1958 Bel Air, but the SS designation didn't arrive until the third-generation Impala in 1961. The second generation, without a Super Sport option, filled the two-year gap as the free-standing Impala model. The first Impala SS model's power output is a story of progression. The 1961 Impala SS arrived with a choice of V8 engines: 348-cubic-inch units rated at 305, 340, or 350 horsepower and a 409-cubic-inch V8 officially rated at 360 horsepower. In 1962, that king-of-the-hill powerplant could also be configured with dual four-barrel carburetors, increasing output to 409 horsepower.

Thanks to solid lifters, dual exhausts, and an 11:1 compression ratio, the 409's output rose to 425 gross horsepower for the 1963 model year. Chevy history buffs may also recall a 1963 Z11 lightweight drag-racing Impala with a 430-horsepower 427-cubic-inch V8. Keep in mind that this one wasn't a Super Sport model, nor was it a part of regular production, as only 57 were ever produced. The 1964 Impala SS continued with the same 409 from the previous year.

Horsepower for the second iteration of the Impala SS was in familiar territory, with peak outputs sitting at 425, but the Impala eventually took a different route to get there. To start, Chevy launched an entirely new Impala with a sleeker exterior and a perimeter frame, ditching the X-type architecture of the outgoing model. The new looks helped the 1965 Impala become the best-selling single model of all time. A record 1,046,514 units were sold, with roughly 23% being SS variants. Impala SS examples from this generation still attract a lot of attention online.

The top engine for the non-SS 1965 Impala was the familiar Turbo-Fire 409-cubic-inch V8, making 400 horsepower. For the SS, Chevy also offered the L78 V8, a 396-cubic-inch V8 rated at 425 gross horsepower. A year later, the L72 427-cubic-inch V8 joined the options list, also rated for up to 425 hp. The powerplant featured a forged crankshaft and pistons, solid lifters, and a dual exhaust system. The SS 427 continued into 1967 and 1968, but with a slightly different L36 engine, still with 427 cubic inches, but now rated at 385 hp. In 1969, output increased to 390 hp.

The final Impala SS came with 303 hp, which is the most of any modern generation. The supercharged V6 in the previous eighth-generation SS was replaced with a naturally aspirated 5.3-liter LS4 V8. That results in a zero-to-60 mph dash of 5.6 seconds, which is on par with a modern-day Mazda Miata – but remember, this was 20 years ago.

That seems straightforward enough, but the final-generation Impala SS has some quirks that don't match its muscle-era badge. Notably, the ninth-generation Impala was front-wheel-drive, and naturally, so was the SS variant. Power traveled through a four-speed automatic transmission, albeit a heavy-duty version. Despite having an upgraded suspension that helped this SS go beyond a rental car-spec version, reviews of the day weren't particularly kind to the SS. In a 2006 road test, Car and Driver stated, "The SS seems to have been created to produce impressive numbers on paper with little regard to driver enjoyment." Nonetheless, the Impala SS's swan song continued through the 2009 model year.

After a quarter-century hiatus, Chevrolet resurrected the Impala SS for the 1994 model year. This time, it was packaged in a rear-wheel-drive sedan with a 260-horsepower 5.7-liter V8 engine under the hood. Engineers didn't have to dig too far into the parts bin. This LT1 V8 already saw duty in the Camaro and Corvette, although there are different LT1 versions over the years. However, the engine in the Impala SS was modified with cast-iron cylinder heads and a different camshaft. It was also tuned for more torque: 330 pound-feet in this application. By today's standards, a 0-to-60 mph dash of seven seconds is nothing exciting, but this was three decades ago, and this Impala SS weighed about 4,300 pounds.

That bulk came from the full-sized Caprice, which underpinned this seventh-generation version. In effect, you could say that Chevrolet made a civilian version of the Caprice police car. The vehicle included an upgraded suspension, improved cooling, larger disc brakes, and a limited-slip differential. The five-spoke aluminum wheels and subtle strips of exterior chrome trim helped distinguish this Impala from its workhorse siblings. Leather upholstery was another clue. For its final production year, 1996, the column-mounted shifter was moved to the center console, and a tachometer was added. That's why low-mileage 1996 Impala SS examples still hold strong collector appeal.

The short-lived eighth-generation Impala SS (2004–2005) stands out for a couple of reasons besides having the lowest engine output (240 horsepower). Namely, it's the only Impala SS with a V6 engine. Yet this is no ordinary six-cylinder powerplant; it's General Motors' 3.8-liter Series II engine with an Eaton supercharger, known for its broad torque band.

This Impala SS is based on the eighth-generation Impala, which was introduced for the 2000 model year as a front-wheel-drive sedan. Fast forward to 2004, and Chevrolet added the SS variant to the lineup, marking the first Impala SS that spins the front wheels. An upgraded four-speed automatic transmission controls the setup, but this Chevy also has larger anti-roll bars, modified springs, and Goodyear performance tires. As a result, 0-60 mph came in 6.5 seconds.

To go beyond a plain-Jane Impala, the automaker also added four round taillights (marketing language called this a Corvette-inspired treatment), black-only exterior paint, a small rear spoiler, leather upholstery, and a slathering of SS badges inside and out. This Impala was axed after 2005 to make way for the aforementioned 2006 Impala SS with a more powerful V8 engine.
