#5511. AI agent tooling provider LangChain secures $300M investment

LangChain Inc., a startup with a set of popular open-source tools for building artificial intelligence agents, has raised $300 million in funding.

The Wall Street Journal reported today that Alphabet Inc.’s CapitalG fund led the round. It was joined by IVP, Sapphire Ventures, GIC and DFJ Growth. LangChain is now worth $3 billion.

San Francisco-based LangChain is best known for the eponymous open-source framework it released in 2022. The software reduces the amount of work involved in building AI agents. LangChain makes it relatively simple to connect an AI agent to a large language model, integrate it with tools and add a system prompt. The framework also enables developers to customize details such as the format of prompt responses.

LangChain’s second open-source tool, LangGraph, is designed for situations where a task is too complicated to be automated by a single agent. LangGraph can link together multiple LangChain-powered agents into a single automation workflow. It can also add in other elements such as a mechanism that requires humans to approve sensitive actions.

The third component of LangChain’s open-source portfolio is Deep Agents. It extends LangChain and  LangGraph with features that make it easier for agents to perform complex work. There’s a virtual file system in which agents can keep data, a work planning tool and a subagent generation feature.

LangChain generates revenue with a suite of paid products called LangSmith. Developers can use it to not only build agents but also to maintain them once they’re in production.

An AI agent usually goes through multiple iterations before it’s released to users. LangSmith enables software teams to save those iterations in a centralized repository. If an update introduces a bug into an agent’s code base, developers can use LangSmith to quickly restore an earlier, bug-free version. Furthermore, they can compare the output quality of different agent versions to identify the one that should be deployed to production.

LangSmith also includes a set of observability features. It generates traces, logs that describe every single step of the workflow through an agent processed a prompt. LangSmith analyzes those traces to find technical issues. From there, it prioritizes them based on their severity and generates code fixes.

After its previous funding round last year, LangChain disclosed that its open-source tools were being downloaded about 90 million times per month. Its LangSmith suite, in turn, is used by Autodesk Inc., Cisco Systems Inc. and a long list of other tech firms.

LangChain reportedly plans to nearly double its headcount to 850 employees by the end of 2027. The company will hire infrastructure experts, AI engineers, salespeople and marketers.

#5510. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5509. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5508. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

#5507. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5506. Surging AI chip revenue and Microsoft deal boost Cerebras Systems stock by 17%

Artificial intelligence chipmaker Cerebras Systems Inc. delivered third-quarter revenue that comfortably beat expectations in its latest financial report today while announcing a new deal with Microsoft Corp., sending its stock up almost 18% in late trading.

The company reported a loss before certain costs such as stock compensation of 67 cents per share, trailing Wall Street’s guidance of a 14-cent-per-share loss, though because of some accounting idiosyncrasies, its numbers are not directly comparable with that guidance. Meanwhile, core adjusted revenue for the period came to $230.9 million, up 70% from a year earlier and surpassing the Street’s target of $214.7 million.

The adjustments in Cerebras’ revenue are the result of some of the quirks in its accounting procedures. The company includes some pass-through revenue that’s subtracted from the total, and it also issues warrants to its major customers, which are then amortized as noncash reductions in revenue based on standard accounting rules, and so these are left out of the adjusted number.

Despite these complexities, investors were clearly impressed with the company’s growth over the quarter, and perhaps even more so by its progress toward profitability. Though Cerebras has not been able to show a profit yet, its adjusted operating margin of -14% was still significantly better than its earlier guidance of -24% from three months earlier.

Chief Executive Andrew Feldman (pictured) told analysts on a conference call that the company has an advantage over its competitors, which are struggling to keep up with customer demand and dealing with growing order backlogs. “I think there is opportunity created, particularly on the hardware side, the sale of hardware, where long lead times in GPUs and more expense creates opportunity for us,” he said, referring to Nvidia Corp.’s graphics processing units.

Cerebras does have a significant backlog for both hardware and cloud services itself, and that number rose from $25 billion in August to $26 billion at the end of the quarter. However, a significant portion of that backlog is related to the deal it struck with OpenAI Group PBC, Feldman said. This implies that other customers don’t have to wait so long for their orders to be processed.

Meanwhile, the chipmaker continues to expand its customer base. After recently signing deals with Amazon Web Services Inc. and Oracle Corp., the company today announced a new customer in Microsoft Corp., although it didn’t provide many particulars about that agreement. The small increase in its backlog doesn’t do much to settle concerns that all of those deals are on the small side, however.

“We believe revenue begins to show up in quarter one of fiscal 2027,” Feldman said after explaining that the agreement with Microsoft was signed and sealed a month earlier.

Feldman also explained that the company is now evaluating its financing options to find ways to meet customer demand and make inroads into its order backlog. It’s not clear what that financing will look like, as capital has become much harder to secure in recent months amid growing nervousness about the insane amounts of cash being spent on AI infrastructure buildouts.

Cerebras may perhaps be able to benefit from the uncertainty at its biggest rival Nvidia, which still dominates the AI chip industry, accounting for over 90% of all chip sales, according to some analysts.

Nvidia is in turmoil following the shocking resignation of its co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. It’s believed that Huang was likely forced to hand in his resignation after being outed for having an affair with an executive of a Singapore-based data center infrastructure firm, who is believed to have been acting as a spy for Chinese intelligence and a conduit for illegal shipments of GPUs into that country. Huang also had a second affair with one of Nvidia’s executives, according to reports that emerged yesterday, and reportedly a third one too.

It may take a while for Cerebras and other chipmakers to take advantage of the disruption to Nvidia, which is seeking to maintain stability through the appointment of longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO, but in the short term its prospects still look good. The company said it anticipates a core gross margin of 47% to 49% in the fourth quarter, with revenue rising to between $310 million and $330 million. Wall Street analysts are looking for a core gross margin of just 42.1% on sales of $271 million.

Moreover, Feldman told analysts on the call that the company believes its revenue will triple by the end of fiscal 2027. If that holds true, it would mean full-year revenue of around $2.85 billion, slightly below Wall Street’s long-term forecast of $2.92 billion in fiscal 2027.

#5505. Low Rates or Lots of Leverage? Buyers Rarely Get Both.

If you’ve been watching mortgage rates lately, you might feel a little stuck. Rates climbed above 7% this year, and a lot of buyers have decided to sit tight and wait for them to come back down.

But rates are only half the story. When you buy a home, you usually get one of two things: low rates or negotiating power. It’s rare to get both at the same time. And right now, you have a lot more of that second one than you might think.

Think back to 2020 and 2021. Rates were near 3%, and buyers rushed into the housing market. Those low rates sounded great, but they came with a catch. There were a lot of buyers just like you that you had to compete with – and there weren’t enough homes for sale to meet that demand.

That’s why homes got multiple offers, buyers paid over asking or waived inspections, and sellers held all the cards. Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com, shows just how one-sided things got:

“Seller’s markets peaked at 98 of 100 metros in spring 2022 after two years of mortgage rates near 3%.”

Then, in the second half of 2022, rates went up. As a result, the number of people buying homes went down, inventory grew, and the balance slowly started tipping from sellers back to buyers. Fast forward to today, and that flip is officially here.

In a recent report, Realtor.com found about two-thirds (66) of the top 100 metros now lean in favor of buyers (see graph below):

And while you may want lower rates, this shift in power has its own perks.

There are more homes for sale than there have been in years. And in a more buyer-friendly market like that, it means sellers have to work harder to get their homes sold. As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Higher inventory and lengthening days on market give buyers improved negotiating power.”

That shows up in the deals buyers are getting. According to Redfin, nearly half of buyers now get some kind of concession from the seller – like help with closing costs, money for repairs, or even the seller paying to buy down your mortgage rate (see graph below):

So when you find a home you love, even if the rate isn’t what you necessarily wanted, there are other levers to pull. Ask about a price cut or a seller-paid rate buydown, too. It could take some of the sting out of today’s rates.

And just in case you’re still thinking you’ll just hold off until rates drop, here’s what you should know. Experts at Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo don’t expect rates to fall much through 2027 (see graph below):

And here’s the whole point. Even if rates did drop in a big way, a lot of buyers would rush back in. More competition means fewer deals, fewer concessions, and sellers getting the upper hand again.

So waiting comes with a trade-off. You might land a better rate down the road, but you’d probably give up the bargaining power you have today.

That doesn’t mean you have to move right now. You should only buy when the numbers work for you. But if you’ve got a real reason to move, today’s leverage could help make your numbers work – even at today’s rates.

Buyers rarely get low rates and strong negotiating power at the same time, and today’s market is handing you the leverage. Connect with a local real estate agent to find homes where sellers may be open to covering a rate buydown or closing costs, so you can see if today’s market can work for your budget.

#5504. Thanksgiving Is the Worst Day of the Year for Cooking Fires—Is Your Kitchen Prepared?

If you’re hosting loved ones this Thanksgiving, now is the time to get your kitchen ready. Otherwise, a nice holiday meal could turn into a costly and dangerous ordeal.

According to the latest data from the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), about 1,139 home cooking fires were reported to U.S. fire departments on Thanksgiving Day 2024.

That’s a 321% increase over the daily average, making Turkey Day the leading day of the year for home cooking fires.

“People don’t ever set out to leave the kitchen unattended, but a minute is all it takes for a grease and oil fire to take over, and there’s a greater risk of that happening on Thanksgiving when every burner is going,” says Payton Kashani, personal injury attorney, president, and managing partner of Sunset West Legal Group PC in Los Angeles.

By preparing your kitchen ahead of time, you can reduce the risk of fires and enjoy a delicious and safe celebration with family.

The NFPA says that unattended cooking is the leading cause of home cooking fires. And that’s quite common on Thanksgiving Day.

Many dishes are usually being cooked at once on the stove, oven, and various countertop appliances. Add in a house full of guests that bring constant interruptions and you’re left with a risky situation.

“Thanksgiving fires aren’t usually about cooking appliances going wrong. They tend to happen in those few minutes when someone steps away to greet a guest at the door. Distractions like this can wind up causing serious burns with long, painful recoveries that shake up a family’s normal life,” explains Amanda Demanda, founder of Amanda Demanda Injury Lawyers in Miami.

Grease and oil fires are particularly concerning because there are so many dishes cooking at the same time.

Additionally, despite the fact that the NFPA strongly discourages the use of oil-based turkey fryers due to fire and burn risk, many people put a frozen or wet turkey into hot oil and cause a fire.

“Fires can also stem from flammable items that get left near the stove, like kitchen towels or food packaging. Loose sleeves may get caught up in the mix, and when things catch on fire, many of the injuries that arise happen from people trying to fight the fire themselves,” adds Demanda.

Before Thanksgiving cooking gets underway, prepare your kitchen and anyone who’s going to be in it or near it.

When you’re frying, boiling, or broiling, stay in the kitchen and set timers so you’ll know when dishes are ready. Once they’re done, check that all burners and your oven are off before you leave the room.

Keep everything that can catch fire well away from the burners, oven, or any other appliance that generates heat. These include towels, paper and plastic bags, oven mitts, wooden utensils, and food wrappers.

“If you’re going to wear long sleeves, make sure they’re close-fitting rather than loose,” says Demanda.

Demanda recommends keeping a lid on standby.

Your fire extinguisher should be within reach as well. Just make sure it’s always near the stove and everyone in your home knows how to use it.

In addition, skip the task of oil-frying your turkey if possible. If you like the taste, buy it already fried or use an oil-less fryer instead.

“In the event you do use a traditional fryer, keep it away from your house, place it on a flat, even surface, and ensure [the turkey] is fully thawed,” says Stephanie Fox, national spokesperson at American Red Cross.

Lastly, direct kids and pets out of the cooking area.

“Kids and pets running around your kitchen are a burn injury waiting to happen, so make sure you have a spot for guests to gather away from your cooking zone,” adds Demanda.

Rich Repich, home services expert at Cinch Home Services in Boca Raton, FL, recommends setting up appetizers and drinks in a different room so guests don't crowd the cook and giving them a separate table to leave any used dishes.

#5503. Today's Market Could Be a Win for Veterans Looking To Buy a Home

If you’re a veteran or active-duty service member who’s been hoping to buy a home, you may have more going for you in today’s housing market than you realize.

VA home loans already come with some pretty powerful benefits. But now, with more homes for sale and buyers having more room to negotiate in many markets, those benefits could go even further.

And if you’ve ever heard that buying with a VA loan is harder, takes longer, or puts you at a disadvantage, there’s something else you should know… a lot of what people believe about VA loans simply isn’t true.

Today, nearly 4 million service members and veterans have an active VA home loan. And according to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), more than 343,000 homes were purchased using VA loan benefits in its most recent reported fiscal year. And it’s easy to see why.

For eligible veterans and service members, VA loans offer advantages that can make buying a home more affordable, including:

No down payment required for many eligible borrowers.

No monthly mortgage insurance, even with no down payment.

Competitive mortgage rates that can help lower monthly payments.

Benefits like this are powerful in any market – and even more so today. That may be why VA loan usage has grown for the last two years in a row.

A few years ago, when homes were getting multiple offers and buyers were competing for nearly every listing, VA buyers sometimes had a harder time getting their offers accepted.

A 2021 survey from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), found 89% of sellers were likely to accept an offer from a buyer using a conventional loan. But only 30% were likely to accept one using an FHA or VA loan.

The reason? Some sellers were concerned that VA financing would take longer, be more difficult to close, and require them to pay more in costs and repairs. But those concerns don’t necessarily reflect how VA loans actually perform.

A white paper from Vetted VA based on 2025 mortgage data busted a lot of VA loan myths:

Myth #1: VA loans get denied more often than other loans.

The Reality: VA loans actually have the lowest denial rate. Just 8.2% of VA purchase applications were denied, compared to 15.0% for conventional loans, 12.8% for FHA loans, and 12.5% for USDA loans.

The Reality: 90% of VA home loan applications that reached underwriting made it to closing, compared to 81% for conventional loans.

The Reality: VA loan appraisals typically take 7–10 business days, similar to conventional and FHA loans.

Myth #4: Sellers have to pay all the closing costs for VA buyers.

The Reality: VA buyers can pay many standard closing costs themselves. Buyers and sellers can also negotiate which eligible costs the seller will cover.

Since there are more homes for sale and fewer buyers competing in many areas, sellers may be more open to different financing options than they were a few years ago. And the opportunity doesn’t stop at getting your offer accepted.

Depending on the house and your local market, you may also be able to negotiate a lower price, ask for repairs, or request help with closing costs.

VA guidelines allow sellers to cover the buyer’s normal closing costs, plus concessions of up to 4% of the home’s value.

Think about what that combination could mean. You may be able to buy with no down payment, avoid mortgage insurance, and negotiate help with some of the other expenses that come with buying a home.

That could mean keeping thousands of dollars in your savings instead of spending them upfront, giving you more breathing room after you get the keys.

#5502. The Housing Market Is on Solid Ground, Even with More Foreclosures

It’s been nearly two decades since the 2008 housing crash, but the word “foreclosure” can still make people uneasy. And if you’re planning a move, you may be wondering if more foreclosures will flood the market with homes for sale – especially if you’ve seen the headlines lately.

Buyers may be hoping for a rush of bargains. Sellers may be bracing for more competition. The latest data points to neither, and knowing why can help you plan your next move with confidence.

Completed foreclosures are up 33% from last year, according to ATTOM. That sounds like a big leap, but context helps.

Even with that increase, foreclosures are still about 26% below where they were in the first half of 2020.

Zoom out further, and today’s activity is a small fraction of what the market saw during the 2008 crash. Lenders completed about 28,000 foreclosures in the first half of 2026, according to ATTOM. Compare that to the crash years in red, when lenders often completed more than 200,000 in the span of a few months (see graph below):

Experts say today’s numbers reflect a housing market that’s still in good shape. As Rob Barber, CEO at ATTOM, explains:

“While some homeowners are still facing financial challenges, overall foreclosure volumes remain well below historical norms and the broader housing market continues to demonstrate resilience.”

And here’s why we can absorb the slight uptick in foreclosures we are seeing.

During the crash, a lot of homeowners either lost their homes to foreclosure or were forced to sell, which left the market overwhelmed with houses for sale. That isn’t happening now.

One way to see this is through months’ supply, which measures how long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace. Four to six months is considered balanced.

Right now, it’s about 4.8 months, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). That’s pretty well-balanced, and less than half of where it peaked around the last crash (see graph below):

If foreclosures were really surging, you’d see it in the number of homes for sale. As Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . a surge of actual foreclosures in 2026 would have easily put the inventory data much higher in 2026.”

Equity is a big reason there’s no surge of distressed sales. Data from the Census Bureau and ATTOM shows nearly two in three homeowners have paid off their mortgage or have more than 50% equity. And Cotality says the average homeowner has about $310,000 in equity.

If a homeowner with equity hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house, pay off the loan, and walk away with money in their pocket instead of facing foreclosure. That’s an option many people didn’t have during the crash. According to HousingWire, nearly one in four homes were underwater back in 2010.

Being underwater means owing more on your mortgage than your home is worth, which makes selling a lot harder. Today, just 2% of homeowners are considered seriously underwater (see graph below):

Not every homeowner has that kind of equity, but most do, and that’s what puts a ceiling on how high foreclosures can go.

If rising foreclosures have you questioning where the housing market is headed, the data says it’s in good shape. The supply of homes for sale is balanced, and most homeowners have plenty of equity.Have questions about what you’re seeing online, your local market, or about how much equity you have? #5501. Planning To Sell in 2027? Start Prepping Now.

If selling your house is on your calendar for 2027, you may be thinking you’ve got plenty of time. Maybe you’re aiming for January. Maybe you’re waiting for spring. Either way, next year probably feels far enough away that getting ready can wait, too.

But waiting until 2027 to sell doesn’t mean waiting until 2027 to get started.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from than they’ve had in years. So, if you want your house to stand out when it’s time to list, a little preparation now can make a big difference later.

As a general rule of thumb, Zillow recommends giving yourself about 2-3 months to get your house ready to list. And that makes sense when you consider that the vast majority of sellers (78%) did at least one home improvement project before their house hit the market.

That gives you plenty of time to decide what to fix, find contractors, get on their schedules, actually make the updates, and get everything ready for photos and showings.

But don’t worry – that doesn’t mean every seller had some big to-do. The most common? Interior painting (see graph below):

That certainly doesn’t mean you need to tackle everything on this list. You may not need to do any of it. But odds are there’s at least one project you’ll want to do. And starting that conversation now gives you a leg up before next year.

While you might have a long list of things you think need updating, that doesn’t mean they’re all worth the time, effort, or money.

An agent will help you figure out which projects deserve a spot on your to-do list based on what buyers want most and what other sellers are doing. That way, you’re not investing in updates that won’t make much of a difference when you sell.

One thing your agent may recommend today is that you go ahead and get a pre-listing inspection. It’s basically your cheatsheet to what a buyer’s inspection may turn up later on.

And now that buyers have more options, they’re pickier – and you don’t want anything popping up in an inspection that could put them off.

For example, you know that HVAC system you’ve been hoping will make it through one more season? Now’s a good time to give it some attention – along with anything else you know needs a little TLC. That way a repair you could’ve handled months ago won’t become a surprise in the middle of your sale.

According to Angi, a pre-listing inspection typically costs $300-600 and that can be money well spent. As the National Association of Realtors (NAR) explains:

“An inspector will be able to give you a good indication of the trouble areas that will stand out to potential buyers, and you’ll be able to make repairs before open houses begin.”

The advantage isn’t just knowing what may come up, but being able to get ahead of it and space out the projects on your own schedule. So you don’t feel stressed during go-time.

But remember, not everything needs to happen right away. Some things are better saved for when you’re closer to listing.

Think deep cleaning, staging, touching up paint, and tidying up the landscaping. Those are the finishing touches that’ll help your house look its best when buyers walk through the door.

But there’s one thing you can start anytime: decluttering. Go ahead and tackle the closets, garage, or storage room you’ve been avoiding. Future you will appreciate having a few less boxes to pack.

The idea isn’t to get everything done today. It’s to spread the work out so you’re not scrambling when listing day arrives. As Redfin puts it:

“Smart preparation leads to a smoother sale, stronger offers, and fewer surprises during closing. . . Homes that are clean, well-staged, priced right, and professionally photographed tend to sell quickly.”

You don't need to spend the rest of the year renovating your house or packing up your life. But you can start making a plan.The earlier you figure out what needs to be done, the more time you'll have to do it right. And that means less rushing, fewer last-minute surprises, and a better chance to make a great first impression when you're ready to sell.Thinking about selling in 2027? #5500. Homeowner’s Massive 60,000-Light Christmas Display Dubbed a Safety Hazard by HOA

'Tis almost the season for goodwill toward all—unless you’re Neil Heuer and his neighbors.

Heuer, a semiretired tech entrepreneur, lives in Aero Plantation, an exclusive fly-in community in Waxhaw, NC, with his wife and their children. Over the past several months, he’s been locked in a battle with Aero Plantation's HOA over his annual Halloween and Christmas displays, which his neighbors say disrupt the neighborhood and make them feel unsafe.

Heuer has been putting on the light shows, which include more than 60,000 lights, choreographed animatronic displays, and coordinated music programming, for the past five years. He estimates he's spent more than $70,000 on the exhibitions.

But after last year’s shows, his neighbors began complaining. Those complaints led to a hearing, a lawsuit, and proposed potential changes to the HOA’s bylaws that would prohibit Heuer’s Christmas and Halloween spectaculars in the future.

For his part, Heuer believes the drama has little to do with the lights and more to do with a golf course dispute and a once-anonymous newsletter he penned to bring HOA issues to light.

"I realize that this is a little unorthodox, but, you know, everybody celebrates things differently," Heuer says of his light displays. "I have friends that celebrate their birthday for the entire month and I might be lucky to have a slice of cake on my birthday, but it doesn't matter. This is my hobby. I love to share it with people. I sit outside and record it myself, and I smile. I'm just so giddy with it."It makes me happy, which is good," he continues. "Especially right now, because I do feel like it's draining. It's been a very draining experience."

Six years ago, Neil and his wife, Stephanie, moved to Aero Plantation, an exclusive fly-in neighborhood with a private airstrip, tennis courts, an equestrian center, and other luxury amenities.

The Heuers' five-bedroom, 8,000-square-foot home sits on 2.36 acres and includes a pool and a four-car garage. Property listing photos show a home hidden in a copse of woods on the edge of a pond.

Heuer tells Realtor.com® he initially got into the holiday displays because of his interest in tech and because his children enjoyed the shows.

“The kids got a kick out of it, and I thought it was cute,” he says.

His neighbors enjoyed the shows, too, he says.“There's a time I can tell you that our neighbors came over and danced in our driveway. We sat and just talked and sat on the front porch and just ... It was really nice," he adds.

Two years ago, though, things took a turn.

Heuer alleges the inciting incident was a disagreement with the HOA board’s vice president over a proposal to “rejuvenate” the community’s golf course. Heuer objected to using reserve funds on the golf course. The vice president offered to pay for the upgrades personally, promising that annual maintenance on the course would be around $8,000, Heuer says.

“After that, I started an anonymous newsletter,” says Heuer. It was meant to “ask questions”

The newsletter "was critical of the HOA, but there was nobody asking these questions. I was anonymous because I really didn't want to receive backlash for asking questions. I didn't want to be on the receiving side of what I'm experiencing now, basically.”

When it was uncovered that Heuer was behind the HOA-critical newsletter, “they basically weaponized the HOA against me,” Heuer says.

At this year’s annual community meeting, when it was revealed that the golf course’s upkeep would run closer to $16,000, he brought up the discrepancy.

“Everybody looked around at me and said, ‘Sit down and shut up,” he says.

Heuer contends that those factors—not the light show itself—have upset his neighbors and led to a hearing earlier this year over alleged HOA violations.

In a letter sent to Heuer in August, the HOA’s legal counsel, Benjamin Karb, wrote that “Inviting unknown members of the public into the subdivision is the type of offensive activity that is a nuisance or annoyance to the neighborhood” and accused Heuer of violating the HOA’s Declaration.

"They believe the roads are private and that nobody belongs here who doesn't live here, I guess," Heuer says. "Let me tell you, 90% of the cars that go by my home I don't recognize. There are people driving by every day who aren't neighbors. And somehow, when they're here to watch my show, they suddenly have a problem. And the people watching my show are families with kids in the backseat."

In September 2026, the HOA held a hearing on the holiday display, alleging it violated the community’s declarations on exterior lighting, signage size, traffic and guest limits, and architectural alterations.

Of major concern was the flow of traffic through the neighborhood by locals looking to see the light show. Aero Plantation is not gated, but it is a private residential community, and the HOA owns and maintains the roads.

In a Sept. 15 letter following the hearing, Karb wrote that when it came to the visitors, the board "did not find a violation exists at this time.”

However, Heuer was found in violation of lighting and signage sizes. The board was unable to make a determination on parking and whether the Heuers had architecturally altered their home’s exterior.

Ironically, the sign that violated the community’s signage limits was one Heuer erected to let visitors know that the off-duty sheriff’s deputies patrolling the neighborhood had been hired by the HOA, not him.

In early October, Heuer filed a lawsuit in North Carolina’s Union Superior Court alleging that the HOA overstepped its authority and failed to provide proper notice and hearing procedures, and that the restrictions being enforced had never been formally adopted in the bylaws.

That case is ongoing, but in the meantime, the HOA board sent out a notice that it was adopting new parking rules in the community.

"While normal visits from family, friends, and personal guests are always welcome, the Rules explicitly address situations where activities conducted, sponsored, or permitted by an Owner attract non-resident traffic—even if the Owner did not personally invite or know each visitor. Owners are held directly responsible for any traffic, stopping, or parking resulting from these activities on our private roads," the notice reads.

Around the same time, a notice was sent to homeowners about two proposed amendments to the bylaws, one of which would establish “standards for public attractions and activities that generate substantial or recurring nonresident traffic within the community.” The other would create “standards for flashing, strobing, pulsating, and high-intensity exterior lighting and authorize the Board to adopt implementing rules consistent with the Declaration.”

The vote on amending the bylaws is scheduled for the end of January, so Heuer plans on going big once more with his holiday display this year.

"Whatever these cockamamie rules that they're trying to change will not apply to this year,” says Heuer.

Realtor.com reached out to the HOA board to inquire about the dispute.

In an emailed response, Aero Plantation HOA President David Arno wrote: “Mr. Heuer filed a lawsuit against the Association, to which the Association will respond through the appropriate legal process. The North Carolina Planned Community Act authorizes an HOA’s members to implement additional changes to a Declaration, which is what members are being asked to decide. The Board does not intend to comment further other than to remind members to voice their opinions by deciding if they want to approve the proposed changes or not.”

After a notice about the proposed amendments were sent out, Heuer emailed his neighbors, imploring them to think twice about adding more amendments to the bylaws.

“Look, you may not like our light show, you may like it. But I don't think we need more rules,” he says.

Regardless of the vote's outcome, Heuer and his wife have decided they’re moving out of Aero Plantation as soon as their youngest daughter, currently a sophomore, graduates from high school.

"There's two things I can assure you," he says. "One is that I will not live here after my daughter graduates. And my next neighborhood will not have an HOA."

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. #5499. Kubernetes now runs containers and VMs side by side

KubeVirt’s graduation from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) marks a turning point in a debate that once pitted containers against virtual machines. A decade on, Kubernetes is becoming one platform for legacy VMs, cloud-native apps and AI.

Enterprises still run much of their IT on VMs, even as AI pushes them toward new infrastructure. Red Hat Inc. is betting they won’t have to choose, with OpenShift 5 managing containers, VMs and AI workloads in one environment. Running two separate systems was never the goal, according to Fabian Deutsch (pictured), director of engineering for OpenShift Virtualization and Modernization and a KubeVirt maintainer at Red Hat.

“But you’ve also got VMs, right, where you’re running applications in the old way that we did for decades before. And do you really want to maintain these two systems?” Deutsch said. “So our vision was, how can we unite those worlds to eventually make it easier to have one paradigm to run both, all these compute workloads on one platform.”

Deutsch spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed KubeVirt’s graduation, running VMs and containers on one Kubernetes platform, AI’s influence on virtualization and what comes next for the project. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes has drawn open-source projects and commercial providers onto a common platform, and AI’s hunger for compute has deepened that pull. Much of KubeVirt’s recent innovation now comes from the AI side, Deutsch explained.

“You don’t want to repave your data center just because you’ve got a new workload that you need to address,” Deutsch said. “So you’re having that flexibility to run it in the way that you need it.”

The CNCF announced the graduation at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, seven years after accepting the project into its sandbox. Next on the list is passing GPUs, CPUs and memory into VMs, while AI is changing how the community values virtualization itself, Deutsch noted.

“There’s a lot of influx of features due to AI, by the way,” Deutsch said. “The isolation model, we didn’t get to it in the beginning, but the isolation of virtualization is helping, right, in the AI age as well.”

The project already runs on edge devices and in the cloud because it offers a consistent API across those footprints, according to Deutsch. Nvidia Corp. was an early adopter, and Microsoft Corp. is now stepping up, he noted.

“I think it’s about getting the right and next generation infrastructure into your house,” Deutsch said. “KubeVirt allows you to carry forward what you’ve got, what you invested in over the past decades, and not to leave it alone because you have to carry it forward.”

#5498. Attached Housing Stands Out in Baltimore’s Housing Market

Annualized new-home sales declined 5.2% in September to 2,613 units. Attached housing accounted for 1,951 sales versus 662 detached sales during the period. However, the Baltimore market is sending mixed signals as 2026 winds down. By comparison, the market’s average new-home sales rate of 2.4 homes per project matched Maryland and remained above the national rate of 2.0.

That aforementioned product split is one of Baltimore’s defining characteristics. Annualized attached sales fell just 0.9% year over year compared with a 16% decline for detached homes as of September data. The strongest sales activity also sits toward the more attainable end of the new home market, with attached homes priced from $350,000 to $450,000 experiencing the most closing activity over the past year.

Related, affordability remains a constraint. As of July, the median new-home closing price stood at $555,337, down 2.9% year over year, compared with $420,000 for existing homes.

The economic backdrop adds another layer. Total nonfarm employment in the Baltimore metro declined 0.6% year over year in August, while the unemployment rate was 4.1%. Households are estimated to decline 0.1% in 2026 and post flat annual growth through 2028.

One potential longer-term catalyst comes from defense manufacturing. Anduril Industries announced a $3.7 billion investment in a high-tech shipyard at Baltimore County’s Tradepoint Atlantic industrial center. The project is expected to create 3,100 direct jobs and support more than 11,000 indirect jobs, while generating more than $2 billion in annual economic output.

Baltimore’s opportunity is therefore less about broad based growth and more about positioning. Ideal locations, attainable price points, and disciplined starts stand out in a market where buyers are still active but increasingly selective.

#5497. Spec Versus Built-to-Order: Builders Navigate a Changing Market

For builders, the push and pull between speculative homes and built-to-order (BTO) homes is a classic struggle, reflecting the desire to balance operational efficiency against market demand. A favorable mix directly dictates a company’s profit margins, inventory risk, and customer satisfaction.

Spec homes allow builders to more directly compete with resale inventory, offering faster move-ins that can capture demand from buyers looking to move quickly. In strong markets, heavier spec exposure can increase sales velocity. In slower markets, builders with large levels of spec inventory are exposed to carrying costs and pricing risk.

A built-to-order approach reduces that inventory risk and offers buyers greater personalization in their final purchase. Built-to-order homes typically carry higher sales prices and translate into healthier margins while requiring buyers to wait longer to move in.

While several companies are steadfast in their approaches, such as the 100% spec commitments of Meritage Homes and CBH Homes and the 70% BTO target set by KB Home, the spec-BTO balance often shifts over time.

In the immediate post-pandemic period, many builders leaned more heavily into spec production. Unprecedented levels of demand and rapidly rising home prices set a backdrop for many large builders to offer more spec and quick move-in (QMI) homes because homes were absorbed at record levels. Similarly, the standardized production and simplified SKU packages helped builders guard against pandemic-related supply chain disruptions and labor shortages.

When mortgage rates began to spike in late 2023, a go-to-market approach with spec production remained prevalent to help buyers with certainty of price and move-in timing. Public builders at the time noted buyers were less willing to commit many months ahead given rate uncertainty and favored move-in ready homes. Builders favoring a heavier spec production mix were able to lean into financing incentives in the form of price cuts and rate buydowns to capture demand as economic uncertainty began to mount.

At the end of 2025 and beginning of 2026, one of the more notable themes to emerge is a more concentrated shift toward a higher built-to-order mix. KB Home began sharing its goal of a 70% BTO mix in the second quarter of 2025, noting the approach is customer-centric and that a design-forward, personalized approach is a differentiator in a market where incentives were prevalent.

“Our buyers choose their lot, floor plan, and personalized finishes. The result is a home that has a real specific value to the people who will live in it,” president and CEO Rob McGibney said during an earnings call with investors. “Homes built to customer specifications do not require heavy incentives to sell.”

Similarly, in the past couple quarters PulteGroup has highlighted its efforts to skew production more toward BTO homes, targeting a 60-40 mix.

“Our decision to build more spec homes once supply chains collapsed and build cycles effectively doubled was the right one at the time, but we much prefer having a growing backlog of sold homes,” PulteGroup president CEO Ryan Marshall shared during a recent earnings call.

The shift is not just occurring among large public builders, with Texas-based Stylecraft Builders reporting a shift toward the BTO model. After carrying essentially no to-be-built volume as recently as 12 to 18 months ago, the company is targeting a goal of 20% to 25% of sales from BTO orders.

Spec-heavy, BTO-heavy, and hybrid operators are all succeeding in the current challenging market. Rather than converging toward a single model, many builders increasingly view spec and BTO homes as complementary tools that can be adjusted based on market conditions, buyer behavior, and community characteristics.

For many builders, spec homes and BTO homes are not an either-or strategy, and a flexible approach that puts buyers front of mind yields the most successful results.

“They serve different customer needs and we want to execute both approaches well,” David Weekley Homes chief operating officer Ladd Fargo tells BUILDER. “The approximate mix depends on the market, buyer behavior, product type, and price point.”

The by-market approach is one that resonates strongly with Trumark Homes. As a private builder that serves as the western hub for Daiwa House, Trumark Homes leans into the local expertise of its division operators to meet the market with the best approach across its operating platforms in California, Colorado, and Washington.

“We know that we have strong operators in all our markets, and we trust our division teams to understand their buyer profiles, have a pulse on the competition, and utilize the data and tools available to plan accordingly,” Trumark Homes chief operating officer Steve Kalmbach says. “We will continue to be nimble and make the best strategic decisions for each community along the way.”

Fred McConnell, vice president of brand and performance marketing at Risewell Homes, tells BUILDER the company has become more intentional about creating built-to-order opportunities while maintaining a strong offering of quick move-in, spec homes. The mixed approach allows Risewell to be both consumer-led and market-responsive while aligning the company’s core brand platform, Built Well to Live Well.

“Our goal is to maintain the flexibility to respond to both the consumer and the dynamics of each individual market and community,” McConnell says.

Huntsville, Alabama-based Davidson Homes has seen a shift toward more BTO homes, but the company’s core strategy has not changed. CEO Brandon Jones says the company continues to meet buyers where they are, offering a solution for those who need to move in 45 days or those who want to choose every detail from homesite to interior finishes. He says the market has not picked a winner between spec or BTO and has instead rewarded builders who are disciplined about using both approaches.

“We start with the buyer, not the model. A lot of our industry has moved to one way of building,” Jones continues. “We’ve kept real personalization on the menu because buyers still want it, and we keep inventory on the ground because some buyers can’t wait. If we get the buyer right, the mix takes care of itself.”

CBH Homes has been a 100% spec builder since 2019, placing high value on the efficiencies gained in the building process and the simplification it provides to the buyer experience. The efficiencies gained early, from purchasing to scheduling trade partners, provide consistency and synergy that allows real value to be passed on to the buyers.

“Being a spec builder allows us to do what we do best: Build amazing homes quickly, efficiently, and at a price that keeps homeownership attainable,” CBH Homes president and owner Corey Barton explains. “Our buyers can walk through a home, see the finishes, know the price, and know when they can move in. There are fewer unknowns.”

In the current market, where some builders are shifting approaches back toward a heavier BTO mix, Barton says CBH Homes still sees value in its 100% spec approach.

“When rates move or the right opportunity presents itself, our buyers don’t have to wait months for their home to be built,” Barton says. “On top of that, we know if a buyer has the option, they will want to make changes. Not allowing change orders allows us to keep costs down and construction efficiency high. Our goal isn’t to give the buyer a thousand decisions to make. It’s to do the work up front and create a beautiful, professionally designed home they can walk into and say, ‘This is it.’”

“Being a spec builder allows us to do what we do best: Build amazing homes quickly, efficiently, and at a price that keeps homeownership attainable.”

Meritage Homes made a similar transition to an all-spec approach in 2016, focusing on the entry-level segment and leaning into competition with resale inventory. The builder’s shorter cycle times allow it to start homes later while also maintaining its 60-day closing guarantee. CEO Phillippe Lord says that its trade relationships and limited SKU counts set it apart from other builders and provide greater certainty to its vendor partners. While the builder has been market responsive and has increased its portfolio of move-up product given market conditions, Meritage Homes remains committed to its 100% spec approach.

Houston-based David Weekley Homes has leaned more heavily into move-in-ready spec homes to respond to a buyer that is placing more value on speed and certainty. Fargo says the shift has been driven by changes in buyer preferences rather than operational considerations.

“In a more uncertain market, many buyers are less willing to commit far in advance. They want to know what they’re buying, what it will cost, and when they can move in,” Fargo explains. “With quick move-in homes, the goal is not simply to build more inventory. It’s to be thoughtful about which homes we start, where we build them, the price points we target, and when the homes will be available.”

Similarly, Kalmbach notes Trumark Homes is seeing more contingent buyers in the current market. For these buyers, knowing what homes are available within a given time frame can be an important factor when they are looking to move but still must sell their previous home. Spec homes represent a solution for this buyer.

For builders that have leaned more heavily into a BTO approach, most cite personalization, design, and customer centricity as core factors. By allowing buyers to choose lots, floor plans, and personalized finishes, says KB Home’s McGibney, the company is best able to serve its customers.

“Buyers are already invested in and feel a connection to the homes they created,” McGibney said. “This is in contrast to a speculative business model where incentives are used to create value. In that model, the builder increases the incentives to the point at which the buyers believe they have been adequately compensated for features and finishes they did not choose.”

Erlanger, Kentucky-based Fischer Homes has seen an increase in interest in BTO homes in 2026, with the builder noting many buyers are placing an emphasis on personalization. BTO homes utilize Fischer Homes’ Design Studio, giving buyers the opportunity to select finishes and details that bring a unique vision to life and allowing the builder to deliver a home that reflects the specific needs and preferences of a particular buyer.

“The visibility and predictability that BTO provides translates directly into more efficient operations and more dependable margins at delivery.”

Beyond design, KB Home’s McGibney said a BTO-forward approach provides visibility, predictability, and limits risk. When a buyer commits and the company locks in a price, the direct costs can be established before a shovel hits the ground and KB Home knows the margin it will achieve at delivery before a home is started.

“We view this as a fundamentally lower risk profile than a speculative model, where a builder starts a home with an assumption for the future sales price and then finds later, at the time of sale, that market conditions may require price reductions or heavy incentives,” McGibney said. “The visibility and predictability that BTO provides translates directly into more efficient operations and more dependable margins at delivery.”

PulteGroup’s shift toward increasing built-to-order homes reflects the preferences of move-up and active-adult buyers. The builder’s lower cycle time allows it to selectively use rate buydowns to facilitate BTO sales while still achieving higher margins than on spec sales.

“[Move-up and active-adult buyers] are individuals who expect choice, and our operating model allows them to choose their preferred lot and select the options and upgrades they desire,” Marshall said.

For luxury builder Toll Brothers, the company can provide a design-forward experience even to spec buyers given its timing and approach to sales. The builder is focused on selling specs as early as possible in the construction cycle to allow personalization through its design studios, providing an experience that is like the BTO experience in all but name.

Several builders say the spec-versus-BTO decision is often less about philosophy and more about the product being sold and the customer buying it.

Decisions are closely tied to what different buyer segments prioritize in the purchase process. For entry-level buyers, value is often concentrated in price, payment certainty, and speed, characteristics that favor a spec approach. Move-up buyers, by contrast, are often purchasing for the home itself and have greater flexibility to prioritize personalization and design choices over speed.

“A first-time buyer is usually solving for payment and timing. A move-up buyer is solving for the home itself,” Jones of Davidson Homes explains. “Spec answers the first. Built-to-order answers the second.”

Kalmbach of Trumark Homes adds that buyers who are seeking customization in the home buying process are more likely to have the resources and time to engage earlier in the purchasing process, beginning with lot selection and continuing through the full design process. Fargo of David Weekley Homes echoes this distinction: standardized, higher-density, and entry-level products generally lend themselves more naturally to move-in-ready construction while higher-priced, customizable homes are better positioned for BTO.

“In general, building from the ground up allows customers the opportunity to personalize their home and participate more fully in the home building process,” says Fargo. “The longer timeline also gives our team members more time to understand the customer, build a relationship with them, and help create a home that is right for them. That relationship and the experience we provide the home building process are things we value.”

Vincent Salandro is an editor for Builder. He earned a B.A. in journalism and a B.S. in economics from American University.

#5496. Meritage, PulteGroup Honor Veterans With Mortgage-Free Homes

Two national home builders are honoring military veterans and their families this fall with the gift of mortgage-free homeownership.

Meritage Homes, through its partnership with Operation Homefront, welcomed U.S. Navy veteran Maggie Coleman and her family to a new home in Gulfport, Mississippi, on Veterans Day. Meanwhile, PulteGroup’s Built to Honor program and Building Homes for Heroes will present mortgage-free homes to U.S. Army veterans Carson Shaw and Ryan Heard and their families ahead of Thanksgiving.

The initiatives provide the families with greater housing stability while building on both companies’ long-standing efforts to support military families.

Meritage Homes and Operation Homefront presented Coleman and her two children with the keys to a new, mortgage-free home during a Veterans Day ceremony Nov. 11.

The approximately 2,000-square-foot, four-bedroom, three-bath home is located in Meritage’s Hidden Trails community in Gulfport, Mississippi. The donation marks the 23rd home Meritage has donated to a military family.

Coleman served 13 years in the Navy, including deployments to Italy and Kuwait. The home allows her family to put down permanent roots in her home state of Mississippi.

“I want to give my children everything I didn’t have,” Coleman said. “I want this home to be a place where my kids and I can share stories and make memories.”

“We’re proud to help welcome the Coleman family home to Gulfport,” Meritage Homes CEO Phillippe Lord said. “We recognize the service and sacrifices she and her family have made, and we’re honored to share in this special moment with them.”

The home was provided through Operation Homefront’s Permanent Homes for Veterans program, which works to help military families achieve long-term stability through mortgage-free housing and other support.

PulteGroup will continue the season of giving Nov. 18, when its Built to Honor program and Building Homes for Heroes present the keys to two mortgage-free homes at the builder’s Spencer Glen community in Riverview, Florida.

The homes will go to U.S. Army Sergeant Carson Shaw and his partner, Annalisa, and Purple Heart recipient U.S. Army Specialist Ryan Heard, his partner, Danielle, and their two children.

Shaw joined the Army in 2019 at age 18 and completed deployments to Iraq and Syria and to Africa. A line-of-duty motor vehicle accident in 2024 left him paralyzed from the waist down. He also lives with the effects of a traumatic brain injury and bilateral hearing loss.

Since his injury, Shaw has participated in six adaptive sports at the Warrior Games and plays wheelchair basketball with the Tampa Strong Dogs. His new accessible home will provide a stable foundation as he pursues a bachelor’s degree in finance and economics.

Heard enlisted in the Army in 2007 and completed two deployments to Iraq and one to Afghanistan. During his 2013 deployment to Afghanistan, an improvised explosive device detonated beneath Heard and three fellow soldiers. Despite sustaining a severe traumatic brain injury, Heard helped treat wounded soldiers and coordinate a medical evacuation before losing consciousness, according to the release.

Heard, who received a Purple Heart, also lives with PTSD, chronic migraines, hearing loss, and chronic pain. His new home will provide him and his family with a mortgage-free place to put down roots.

The two homes continue a significant milestone for PulteGroup’s Built to Honor program. Since its launch in 2013, PulteGroup has built and donated more than 100 mortgage-free homes valued at over $40 million to veterans and their families.

Building Homes for Heroes is also celebrating its 20th anniversary and expects to reach its milestone 500th home in December.

#5495. Savannah Guthrie Extends NBC News Contract as Search Continues for Her Mother, Nancy Guthrie

To see our latest updates on the Nancy Guthrie case, please click here.

Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract with NBC News, solidifying her spot as a co-anchor on “Today.”

The decision comes months after it was previously reported that the host was expected to “never return” to her on-air role, as she waited for answers regarding the Feb. 1 kidnapping of her mother, Nancy Guthrie.

Guthrie, 54, returned to the show—and her home in New York City—after a six-week hiatus.

“Savannah is the best in the business,” a Page Six source said on Nov. 12. “We want her to stay for as long as she wants to stay.”

In 2024, the outlet previously reported that the journalist—who joined “Today” in June 2011 as chief legal correspondent and a co-host of the show’s third hour—earns between $7 and $8 million annually.

A People magazine source described Guthrie as “not only so unbelievably strong,” but as “the glue that keeps the show together.”

Authorities are still investigating her 84-year-old mother’s abduction from her Tucson, AZ home—and Guthrie continues to feel the weight of the tragedy each day.

“It’s always with me,” she shared during a June episode of the morning news show. “I cry every morning on the way to work, and I cry every morning on the way home.”

The most recent update in the case comes with a former FBI agent’s revelation that she had received four disturbing ransom messages concerning Nancy’s disappearance. The former agent, Jennifer Coffindaffer, shared she had been targeted by individuals claiming to have information about the disappearance, and demanding cryptocurrency in exchange for her return.

Coffindaffer could not confirm the authenticity of the communications, and believed the messages may have been sent by individuals hoping to capitalize on the high-profile investigation.

The former agent passed the communications to the FBI. The bureau was able to confirm that the cryptocurrency wallet address provided did not correspond with those associated with previous ransom notes investigators considered to be potentially authentic.

Anyone with any information about Nancy Guthrie's case should call 1-800-CALL-FBI, 520-351-4900, or 88-CRIME, or visit tips.fbi.gov.

Coffindaffer had initially chosen not to share the emails publicly, but had a change of heart after Lauren Serpa, a woman who lives near Nancy’s home, had received and shared similar communications—which included unsettling photos of Nancy and religious references that appeared to be tailored to the family’s Catholic faith.

Coffindaffer had become concerned that others following the investigation could become targets for individuals seeking money.

Guthrie has made a series of public pleas, in hopes of sharing a “very specific message” with the individuals who could have information about her mother’s disappearance.

“It has been months since our mom was taken from us. Our family is in agony. We are in a nightmare that will not end. Nothing about our situation has changed. We have done our part. But we will never stop looking for her,” she said in a July statement shared to Instagram.

“We will always ache for her and feel that hole in our hearts,” she continued. “The world can be a cruel and unforgiving place, and I know that you have tried to do things the right way, so I am asking you, begging you to do the right thing now.”

Guthrie closed the statement with an ask for help, and a promise that it’s “never too late to do the right thing.”

“I always believe there is a way home,” she said. “Please make the right choice.”

Nancy was first reported missing at around 12 p.m. local time on Feb. 1, around 14 hours after she was dropped off at the property following a family dinner. When she failed to turn up at her usual church gathering on Sunday, her friends alerted her family, who found her home was empty.

Officials have noted during a Feb. 5 media briefing that, while times are approximate, the team pieced together several pieces of evidence to indicate Nancy's movements—and the timeline of her apparent abduction.

5:32 p.m. Nancy travels to Annie's house in an Uber for "dinner and playing games with the family."

9:48 p.m. A garage door at Nancy's house opens when she was dropped off at the property by her daughter.

9:50 p.m. The garage door closes, indicating that Nancy was inside the home.

1:47 a.m. Nancy's doorbell security camera is disconnected.

2:12 a.m. Movement is detected on a security camera at the home. No footage of this is currently available.

2:28 a.m. Nancy's pacemaker app indicates that the device has been disconnected from her phone.

11:00 a.m. Nancy fails to arrive at the home of a friend, where she had been due to watch a church service livestream.

11:56 a.m. Nancy's family travels to her home to check on her and finds the property empty.

12:03 p.m. The family calls 911 to report Nancy missing.

12:14 p.m. Police officers arrive at Nancy's home.

Police uncovered evidence inside the property suggesting the 84-year-old was "taken" from her home against her will, and "harmed" during the alleged "abduction."

Law enforcement still had no suspects, but were investigating multiple ransom notes and tips providing potentially helpful information.

Savannah Guthrie releases her first public plea, asking for help in finding her missing mother.

Authorities detained a man for questioning after reviewing footage of a masked, armed intruder tampering with a security camera outside of Nancy's home. It was unclear if the person who was questioned was the same individual from the footage.

The FBI announced it was conducting a new "extensive" search for Nancy in the area surrounding her Arizona home. The Pima County Sheriff's Department noted it had received nearly 18,000 calls about the case, and that "several hundred detectives and agents" were assigned to the ongoing investigation.

The Guthrie family was officially cleared as suspects.

Law enforcement officials revealed the kidnapper had a "target."

"I think this was an individual who had a target for whatever reason, and he has made it tough, but I've got some pretty tough investigators, too," Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos shared.

Guthrie broke down in tears as she offered a reward of up to $1 million for anyone who was able to provide information leading to the recovery of her mother.

It was reported that the FBI decided to pull nearly all of the agents assigned to the case out of Tucson and return them to the agency's Phoenix headquarters.

A man was arrested outside of Nancy's home on DUI charges after he was seen driving past the property "50 to 100 times" while looking at a photo of the missing woman on his phone. A spokesperson confirmed the arrest, but noted it had no connection to Nancy's case.

Additional evidence was identified—ranging from DNA found on various objects and thumbnail images from motion-activated cameras in Nancy's backyard—but the search continues.
